dating_basis: Gongyang/Guliang: Xiang 21; Shiji: Xiang 22.
title_en: Birth of Confucius
summary_en: Born in the state of Lu to a minor military family; the exact year differs by a year between the commentaries and Sima Qian.

dating_basis: Shiji 47 sequence after the Jiagu meeting (-500) and the dismantling of the three fortresses (-498); Zuozhuan is silent on the departure.
title_en: Confucius leaves Lu and begins fourteen years of wandering
summary_en: After failing to reform Lu's politics he departed with disciples, visiting Wei, Song, Chen, Cai and Chu in search of a ruler who would employ him.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan Ai 11: Lu summons him with gifts and he returns.
title_en: Confucius returns to Lu
summary_en: Recalled by Lu after his disciple Ran Qiu's military success; he spent his last years editing texts and teaching.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan Ai 16, summer, fourth month, day jichou.
title_en: Death of Confucius
summary_en: Recorded in the Lu annals with the Duke's lament; disciples mourned three years at his grave.

dating_basis: Shiji 63 and 47; no contemporary source. Placed within Confucius's adult life for display only.
title_en: Confucius consults Laozi on ritual (traditional)
summary_en: Sima Qian reports that Confucius travelled to the Zhou capital and questioned Laozi about the rites, and left saying Laozi was like a dragon. The story is unverifiable and may be a later Daoist polemic.

dating_basis: Death year follows Bechert's short chronology; traditional -543 or -483. Place from DN 16.
title_en: The Buddha's death (parinibbana) at Kusinara
summary_en: After a final journey from Rajagaha, the Buddha died between two sal trees at Kusinara; his last words urged diligence. The date is the anchor for all Indian chronology and is uncertain by a century.

dating_basis: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 Rev. 11'-13', re-read at livius.org on 2026-10-14 (Sophia r12-3): in the seventh year, in Kislimu, the king of Akkad marched to the Hatti-land, besieged the city of Judah, and on the second day of Addaru seized the city and captured the king; he appointed a king of his own choice and sent heavy tribute to Babylon. The page glosses the year as 598/597 and the month as February/March 597. The day-date is Parker & Dubberstein 1942, read this session: year 7 of Nebuchadnezzar II has a second Ululu (p. 4 lists 'Ululu II, 7th year'), so in their table (p. 25) Addaru of that year begins on 15 March 597 and its second day is 16 March 597 (the Babylonian day began at the preceding sunset). 2 Kings 24:10-17, read this session in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version, tells the same capture: the siege (24:10-11); Jehoiachin goes out to the king of Babylon, who 'took him in the eighth year of his reign' (24:12); the king, his household and 'ten thousand captives' are carried to Babylon (24:14-16); Mattaniah is made king as Zedekiah (24:17). Kings' eighth year against the Chronicle's seventh is recorded on E_IL_037 and not resolved here; the single year follows the Chronicle's dated day. The summary's Ezekiel: he names himself 'the priest' (Ezekiel 1:3) and counts his years by 'our captivity' (33:21, 40:1), which 1:2 calls king Jehoiachin's (all read this session).
title_en: First deportation from Jerusalem; Jehoiachin and elite exiled to Babylon
summary_en: Nebuchadnezzar took the city, deported the king and thousands of the elite, including the priest Ezekiel, and installed Zedekiah.

dating_basis: Ezekiel 1:1-2, re-read at its locator on 2026-10-14 (Sophia r12-3) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version: 'in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month' (1:1), 'which was the fifth year of king Jehoiachin's captivity' (1:2). The 'thirtieth year' of 1:1 has no stated era and is not used. The captivity begins with the capture ABC 5 Rev. 12' dates to 2 Addaru of Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year (16 March 597; E_IL_001). Counting Babylonian years from Nisan, a stamp in months 1-9 of captivity-year N falls in the Julian year 598 minus N, and one in months 10-12 in 597 minus N (the conversion every dated Ezekiel row carries); month 4 of year 5 gives 593. The summary's wording is Ezekiel 1:1 and 1:3, re-read at its locator on 2026-10-08 (Sophia r11-5) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version.
title_en: Ezekiel's vision by the Chebar canal
summary_en: Among the captives by the river Chebar, in the land of the Chaldeans, the heavens were opened and Ezekiel saw visions of God. The exact place (Tel-abib on the Chebar canal near Nippur) is not securely located; Babylon used as the region's proxy point.

dating_basis: 2 Kings 25:8-9, re-read at its locator on 2026-10-14 (Sophia r12-3) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version: 'in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar', Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem 'and he burnt the house of the LORD'. Jeremiah 52:12-13 (read this session) gives the same nineteenth year and fifth month, on the tenth day. The Babylonian Chronicle for this year is not preserved: the ABC 5 text at livius.org, re-read this session, breaks off in Nebuchadnezzar's eleventh year (594/593). WHY TWO YEARS: counted as the Chronicle counts (seventh year = 598/597, ABC 5 Rev. 11'), the fifth month of the nineteenth year begins on 9 August 586 in Parker & Dubberstein 1942's table (p. 26, read this session); but Kings puts the 597 capture in the eighth year (2 Kings 24:12) where the Chronicle has the seventh, and on that count Kings' nineteenth year is the Chronicle's eighteenth, whose fifth month begins on 20 August 587 (same page). Neither count is chosen; the range holds both. The summary rests on 2 Kings 25:1-4 (the siege from the ninth year, tenth month, tenth day (25:1), to the eleventh year of Zedekiah (25:2), when on the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was sore and the city was breached (25:3-4; JPS 1917 brackets 'fourth' as supplied there, and Jeremiah 52:6, read, has it in the text): about eighteen months on a year counted from the spring), 25:9 (the burning), and 25:7, 25:21 and 25:22 (Zedekiah blinded and taken to Babylon; 'So Judah was carried away captive out of his land'; Gedaliah made governor over those left), all read this session.
title_en: Fall of Jerusalem and destruction of the First Temple
summary_en: After an eighteen-month siege the city fell, the Temple was burned and Judah ceased to exist as a kingdom.

dating_basis: Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) at livius.org, A. K. Grayson's translation (read 2026-10-13; copyright, cited and paraphrased): iii 14-16, Sippar is captured without battle on the fourteenth day, and on the sixteenth Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, and the army of Cyrus enter Babylon without battle; iii 18, on the third day of the month Arahsamna Cyrus enters Babylon. Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 11 (read 2026-10-13) read the same chronicle lines as Sippar falling VII/14/17 (11 October 539), Babylon VII/16/17 (13 October) and Cyrus entering VIII/3/17 (29 October 539); the seventh month is Tashritu, which the livius translation does not name at these lines. The range is the single year -539. Cyrus's own account is the Cyrus Cylinder (Rogers 1912, p. 381, lines 12-17, read 2026-10-13): Marduk sought a righteous prince, called Cyrus by name, and 'Without battle and conflict he permitted him to enter Babylon'. (Until 2026-10-13 this basis cited iii 15-16 for both entries; Cyrus's own entry is at iii 18.)
title_en: Cyrus takes Babylon
summary_en: Persian forces entered Babylon without a fight, and Cyrus himself entered the city some days later. On his own cylinder he says that Marduk chose him and let him enter Babylon without battle. The Neo-Babylonian empire ended and the Judean exiles gained a new overlord.

dating_basis: Ezra 1:1, re-read at its locator on 2026-10-14 (Sophia r12-3) in JPS 1917 through the Sefaria API (version 'The Holy Scriptures: A New Translation (JPS 1917)', license 'Public Domain' as served), identical to the Sefaria-Export file of the same version: 'in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia' the LORD stirred up his spirit, and he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and put it also in writing; the proclamation follows at 1:2-3 (Q_063). The first year is read, as this row always has, as the first year of Cyrus's rule in Babylon. Parker & Dubberstein 1942, read this session: Cyrus entered Babylon on VIII/3 of his accession year, 29 October 539 (p. 11, from the Nabonidus Chronicle), and his first year runs from 1 Nisanu, 24 March 538, to the end of Addaru, about 11 March 537 (table, p. 27). The range therefore holds both Julian years. The single year 538 first given here was the first part of that year only, and no derivation was recorded for it. The summary's 'Second Isaiah had already hailed him as God's anointed' is Isaiah 45:1, 'Thus saith the LORD to His anointed, to Cyrus' (read this session), inside W_ISAIAH_40_55's window (-550/-539).
title_en: Cyrus's decree permitting the Judeans to return and rebuild the Temple
summary_en: Per Ezra, Cyrus proclaimed that the exiles could go up to Jerusalem and rebuild; Second Isaiah had already hailed him as God's anointed.

dating_basis: Behistun DB I 11-15 (dates by Babylonian month); Herodotus 3.61-79 gives the narrative. The day: Behistun col. I §13 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-10-13) has Darius slay Gaumata when '10 days in the month Bagayadi were completing their course', at the stronghold Sikayauvati in the province Nisaya in Media; Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12 (read 2026-10-13) convert this to 29 September 522 (VII/10).
title_en: Darius kills Gaumata and seizes the throne
summary_en: Darius and six conspirators killed, at a stronghold in Media, the man ruling as Cyrus's son Bardiya, whom Darius branded an impostor and a Lie.
note: Place: the fortress Sikayauvatish in Media, not securely located; coordinate left blank. (Moved here from the summary on 2026-10-13.)

dating_basis: Composed after the rebellions it records: Darius says he fought them 'in the same year after that I became king' (Behistun col. IV §2, Tolman 1908, read 2026-10-13), and Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 14 (read 2026-10-13) date the capture of the last Babylonian rebel, Nebuchadnezzar IV, to 27 November 521. Neither bound of -520/-518 is derived from these readings: they place the composition after late November 521, which the lower bound respects, and give no upper limit. The three languages are those of Tolman's headnote to the inscriptions of Behistan (read 2026-10-13): four columns of Persian text with a fifth to their right, three columns of the Elamite version, and the Babylonian version on a projecting block. (Until 2026-10-13 this basis also said that the Aramaic copy at Elephantine is later; no source read for this corpus carries that copy, and the clause is withdrawn.)
title_en: Darius has the Behistun inscription carved
summary_en: On a cliff above the road from Babylon to Ecbatana, Darius set out his year of victories in three languages, crediting Ahura Mazda and condemning his enemies as followers of the Lie.

dating_basis: Archon year of Solon per Ath. Pol. and the archon list; some scholars place the reforms later (-592/-591). The summary's departure is Constitution of the Athenians 11 (Kenyon, read 2026-10-11, this session): he 'set off on a journey to Egypt ... giving out that he should not return for ten years'.
title_en: Solon's archonship and reforms
summary_en: Solon cancelled debts, abolished enslavement for debt, and redefined political rights by wealth class; he then left Athens, saying he would not return for ten years, so that he could not be pressed to change the laws.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 21 (Kenyon, MIT plain text, read 2026-10-11, this session): 'three years after the expulsion of the tyrants, in the archonship of Isagoras', Cleisthenes distributed the population into ten tribes and made the Council five hundred. With the expulsion in the archon year 511/510 (E_GR_012), three years later is 508/507; the archonship of Isagoras is not converted here from the archon list. Herodotus 5.66.2 (Godley, read this session) tells the reform without a year: Cleisthenes 'took the commons into his party' and 'divided the Athenians into ten tribes instead of four'; 5.69.2 likewise.
title_en: Cleisthenes' reforms found the Athenian democracy
summary_en: After expelling the Spartan-backed Isagoras, Cleisthenes reorganised the citizen body into ten tribes and a Council of Five Hundred; Herodotus says he 'took the commons into his party'.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.1: floruit in the 69th Olympiad. A floruit, not an event; displayed as an activity band. The summary's book in the temple of Artemis is DL 9.6 (read 2026-10-11, this session): 'This book he deposited in the temple of Artemis'.
title_en: Heraclitus active at Ephesus
summary_en: Wrote a book he deposited in the temple of Artemis; taught that everything flows and that a common logos underlies apparent opposites.

dating_basis: Thucydides 2.34: the first winter of the war.
title_en: Pericles delivers the funeral oration
summary_en: Speaking over the first war dead, Pericles described Athens as a city whose constitution 'favours the many instead of the few'. Thucydides reconstructed the speech, as he admits.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.44 (Hicks; PerseusDL perseus-eng2, TEI section 2.5.44, read 2026-10-11, this session, with the Greek at the same section): Socrates 'died in the first year of the 95th Olympiad at the age of seventy'. On calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD, Ol. 95.1 = 400/399 BCE, so the range is -400/-399. Diogenes names no archon here, and the name Laches occurs nowhere in book 2 of either file, so no archon is given. The summary rests on Plato, Apology 24b-c (the sworn charge, that he 'corrupts the youth and does not believe in the gods the state believes in') and 37c-e (he asks 'Shall I then propose exile as my penalty?' and rejects it), Fowler, PerseusDL, read this session; and on Diogenes Laertius 2.42, read the same day: 'He was put in prison, and a few days afterwards drank the hemlock'.
title_en: Trial and execution of Socrates
summary_en: Accused of corrupting the young and of not believing in the gods the city believed in, Socrates was condemned. In Plato's Apology he refuses to propose exile as his penalty; Diogenes Laertius has him put in prison, where he drank the hemlock.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Xiang year 30 (= -543): 子產使都鄙有章，上下有服，田有封洫，廬井有伍 — Zichan gave capital and countryside their proper distinctions, ranks their proper dress, fields their boundary ditches, and households their groups of five. The same passage records the two street songs, one in his first year cursing him and one in his third thanking him. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Zichan takes charge of Zheng and reorders it
summary_en: Zichan reorganised land, households and rank in the small state of Zheng. The Zuozhuan preserves what the streets sang about him: in year one, 'they have taken our clothes and taxed our fields — who will kill Zichan? I will join him'; in year three, 'Zichan taught my sons and made my fields grow — if Zichan dies, who will follow him?'

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 4 (= -538): 鄭子產作丘賦。國人謗之 — Zichan instituted the qiu levy and the people of the capital abused him; he answered 苟利社稷，死生以之 ('if it profits the altars of the state, I will do it living or dying') and 民不可逞，度不可改 ('the people cannot be indulged, the measure cannot be changed'). Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Zichan imposes the qiu levy and refuses to withdraw it
summary_en: A new military tax on land units brought public abuse — a lampoon called his father dead in the road and the son a scorpion's tail. Zichan's reply, that he would do what served the state living or dying and would not change the measure to please anyone, became a stock quotation for the official who governs against popular feeling.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 6 (= -536): 三月，鄭人鑄刑書 — 'in the third month the men of Zheng cast the penal code'. The same entry carries Shuxiang's letter of protest in full and Zichan's short reply. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Zheng casts the penal code in bronze
summary_en: For the first time in the Chinese record a state published its criminal law, cast on bronze where anyone could read it. Shuxiang of Jin wrote to say it would ruin the state: once people know the exact rules they stop fearing their superiors, argue from the text and litigate over the point of an awl. Zichan answered in two sentences that he could not save later generations, only this age.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 3 (= -539), the conversation at the Jin court: Yan Ying says of Qi 此季世也 ('this is a last age') and 齊其為陳氏矣 ('Qi will belong to the Chen'), describing how the Chen lend by the large measure and collect by the small; Shuxiang answers 雖吾公室，今亦季世也 ('so too, now, is our own ducal house') and lists the noble clans sunk to servitude. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Yan Ying and Shuxiang agree that both their states are finished
summary_en: Two of the ablest ministers of the age met and told each other the truth: in Qi the ruling house was losing the people to a rival family that lent generously and collected lightly, and in Jin the old clans had sunk to servants while power moved to private households. Both were right. The passage is the clearest contemporary statement that the Zhou order was ending.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 20 (= -522): 鄭子產有疾 ... 疾數月而卒 — he fell ill, gave Zi Taishu his advice about leniency and severity, and died after some months; and at the end of the passage 及子產卒，仲尼聞之，出涕曰：「古之遺愛也。」 Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Death of Zichan; Confucius weeps at the news
summary_en: On his deathbed Zichan told his successor that only a man of real virtue can govern by leniency; fire is fierce and people keep away from it, water is gentle and people drown in it. His successor governed leniently, banditry broke out, and he wished he had listened. When Confucius heard of Zichan's death he wept and called him a legacy of love from the ancients.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 25 (= -517), at the meeting at Huangfu: Zhao Jianzi asks about the ceremonies of bowing and yielding and is told 是儀也，非禮也 ('that is deportment, not ritual'); asked what ritual is, Zi Taishu answers 吉也聞諸先大夫子產曰，夫禮，天之經也，地之義也，民之行也 — quoting the dead Zichan. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Zi Taishu tells Zhao Jianzi what ritual is, quoting the dead Zichan
summary_en: Asked about court etiquette, the envoy of Zheng distinguished deportment from ritual and then gave the definition he had from Zichan: ritual is the constant of heaven, the rightness of earth and the conduct of the people. It is the fullest statement in the Zuozhuan of li as cosmic order rather than good manners, and the ancestor of the Confucian use of the word.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao year 29 (= -513): 冬，晉趙鞅，荀寅，帥師城汝濱，遂賦晉國一鼓鐵，以鑄刑鼎，著范宣子所謂刑書焉 — in winter Zhao Yang and Xun Yin levied a quantity of iron from the state of Jin and cast a penal cauldron inscribed with the code of Fan Xuanzi; 仲尼曰：「晉其亡乎失其度矣。」 — Confucius said Jin would perish, having lost its measure. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Jin casts its penal code on a cauldron and Confucius condemns it
summary_en: Twenty-three years after Zheng, the great northern state did the same thing, and this time it is Confucius who objects: with the law on the cauldron the people look to the cauldron, and if the ranks are no longer respected there is no state left to govern. The Zuozhuan gives the argument against published law twice, from two different men, which is a measure of how new it felt.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 4 (= -506), Chunqiu classic entry: 冬，十有一月，庚午，蔡侯以吳子及楚人戰于柏舉，楚師敗績。楚囊瓦出奔鄭。庚辰，吳入郢 — in the eleventh month, on the day gengwu, the marquis of Cai with the viscount of Wu fought the men of Chu at Boju and the Chu army was routed; on the day gengchen Wu entered Ying. title_en: Wu breaks Chu at Boju and enters the Chu capital
summary_en: A southern kingdom the northern states had barely counted marched into the capital of the greatest power in the Chinese world. Wu Zixu, an exile from Chu, had planned it. Twelve years later, with a Wu army in Chen and the ministers of Chu afraid, the Zuozhuan has the Chu minister Zixi explain that defeat: King Helü ate one dish, sat on no double mat, and in the field would not eat until the cooked food had been shared out.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 4 (= -506), in the narrative that follows the classic entry and runs into the next year: 申包胥如秦乞師 ... 立依於庭牆而哭，日夜不絕聲，勺飲不入口七日。秦哀公為之賦無衣，九頓首而坐。秦師乃出 — Shen Baoxu went to Qin to beg an army, stood leaning against the courtyard wall weeping day and night without stopping and without a mouthful of water for seven days; Duke Ai of Qin recited the ode 'No Clothes' for him, and the army of Qin marched out. The Zuozhuan places the Qin relief in the following year (Ding 5), hence -505. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). title_en: Shen Baoxu weeps for seven days at the court of Qin and Chu is saved
summary_en: With the Chu capital occupied and the king a fugitive, one official went to Qin and simply refused to stop crying until he got an army. He got one, and Chu survived. The seven days at the wall became the standard Chinese image of an appeal that succeeds through sheer persistence.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 10 (= -500): 夏，公會齊侯于祝其，實夾谷。孔丘相 — in summer the duke met the marquis of Qi at Zhuqi, that is Jiagu, with Kong Qiu as master of ceremonies. The same passage has Confucius stop an armed ambush by appealing to what is auspicious before the spirits and proper between men, refuse an unequal clause in the covenant, and decline the banquet; 齊人來歸鄆、讙、龜陰之田 — the men of Qi returned the fields of Yun, Huan and Guiyin. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Confucius as master of ceremonies at the meeting of Jiagu
summary_en: The one moment in the annals where Confucius acts on the public stage. At a summit between Lu and the far stronger Qi he turned back an armed intimidation by naming it a breach of ritual, refused a one-sided clause in the treaty, and Lu got its territory back. Ritual used as a diplomatic weapon, in the source closest to the event.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 12 (= -498): 仲由為季氏宰。將墮三都 — Zhong You (Zilu) became steward of the Ji family and the dismantling of the three fortress-towns was undertaken; Hou and Bi were pulled down, the men of Bi attacked the duke and were beaten at Gumie on Confucius's order, and 冬，十二月，公圍成，弗克 — in the twelfth month the duke besieged Cheng and failed. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: The attempt to pull down the three fortresses of Lu
summary_en: The great families of Lu each held a walled town that their own stewards kept rebelling from. The policy of dismantling all three — carried out with Confucius's disciple Zilu as the Ji family's steward, and with Confucius himself giving a battlefield order — took two of the three and then failed at the third. It is the high-water mark of Confucius's practical politics.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ding year 14 (= -496): 吳伐越，越子勾踐禦之，陳于檇李 — Wu attacked Yue and Goujian met it in battle order at Zuili; after his condemned men cut their own throats in front of the Wu line, 靈姑浮以戈擊闔廬，闔廬傷將指，取其一屨。還卒於陘，去檇李七里 — Linggufu struck Helü with a dagger-axe, taking off his big toe and one shoe, and he died at Xing on the way back, seven li from Zuili. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Yue beats Wu at Zuili and King Helü dies of a wound
summary_en: Goujian broke the Wu line by sending ranks of condemned men to cut their own throats in front of it. Helü was wounded in the foot and died on the road home. The Zuozhuan adds that Fuchai posted a man at his gate to shout at him every time he passed: 'Fuchai! Have you forgotten that the king of Yue killed your father?'

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 1 (= -494): 吳王夫差敗越于夫椒，報檇李也，遂入越，越子以甲楯五千，保于會稽，使大夫種因吳大宰嚭以行成 — King Fuchai of Wu defeated Yue at Fujiao in revenge for Zuili, entered Yue, and Goujian held Kuaiji with five thousand armoured men and sued for terms through the Wu chief steward Bo Pi. The same entry carries Wu Zixu's speech against granting them. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Fuchai defeats Yue at Fujiao and spares Goujian on Kuaiji
summary_en: Goujian was beaten down to five thousand men on a mountain and sued for peace. Wu Zixu told Fuchai that Yue was a disease of the heart and belly and that to conquer and not take was to defy heaven and feed an enemy; he cited a legend about a dynasty restored from a single district. Fuchai spared Yue, and lost his kingdom to it twenty-one years later.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 11 (= -484): 吳將伐齊，越子率其眾以朝焉 ... 弗聽，使於齊 ... 反役，王聞之，使賜之屬鏤以死 — as Wu prepared to attack Qi the ruler of Yue came to court with gifts and Wu Zixu alone was afraid; his warning was rejected, he was sent as envoy to Qi, and on his return the king sent him the Zhulou sword that he might die. His last words: 樹吾墓檟 ... 吳其亡乎三年，其始弱矣。盈必毀，天之道也。 Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Wu Zixu is sent a sword and dies
summary_en: Wu Zixu told Fuchai that Yue's gifts were fattening Wu for slaughter, and that a doctor who leaves some of the disease has never cured anyone. He was given a sword and ordered to kill himself. He asked for catalpas to be planted on his grave so there would be timber for Wu's coffin, and said what is full must be broken — that is the way of heaven.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 11 (= -484), Chunqiu classic entry: 甲戌，齊國書帥師及吳戰于艾陵，齊師敗績，獲齊國書 — on the day jiaxu, Guo Shu of Qi led an army and fought Wu at Ailing; the Qi army was routed and Guo Shu taken. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Wu destroys the army of Qi at Ailing
summary_en: The victory that made Wu, for a moment, the leading power in the Chinese world, and the campaign that Wu Zixu had said would gain nothing but stony ground. It emptied the kingdom while Yue rebuilt behind it.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 11 (= -484): the Qi invasion of Lu, in which Ran Qiu argues the head of the Ji family into fighting — 季孫之甲七千，冉有以武城人三百，為己徒卒 — and commands the left wing with three hundred men of Wucheng as his own troops. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Ran Qiu holds off the Qi invasion at the suburbs of Lu
summary_en: Confucius's disciple, as steward of the most powerful family in Lu, argued his masters into resisting a Qi invasion instead of buying it off, and led the left wing himself. The victory is why Lu recalled Confucius from exile the same year (E_CN_003).

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 13 (= -482): 夏，公會單平公、晉定公、吳夫差于黃池 — in summer the duke met Duke Ping of Shan, Duke Ding of Jin and Fuchai of Wu at Huangchi; and in the same year 六月，丙子，越子伐吳 ... 丁亥，入吳 — in the sixth month, on the day bingzi, the ruler of Yue attacked Wu, and on the day dinghai entered the Wu capital; the Wu king had seven men beheaded in his tent to stop the news spreading. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Fuchai claims the leadership at Huangchi while Yue takes his capital
summary_en: At the moment Fuchai stood at the northern summit disputing precedence with Jin, Goujian's army walked into the Wu capital and captured the crown prince. Fuchai executed the messengers to keep it quiet long enough to finish the ceremony. The Zuozhuan reports both halves under the same year, without comment.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 14 (= -481): 甲午，齊陳恆弒其君壬于舒州。孔丘三日齊，而請伐齊三 — on the day jiawu Chen Heng of Qi murdered his ruler Ren at Shuzhou; Confucius fasted for three days and three times asked Duke Ai to attack Qi. The duke sent him to the Ji family; Confucius declined and said afterwards that, having once ranked among the great officers, he had not dared keep silent. title_en: Chen Heng murders the duke of Qi and Confucius asks Lu to punish him
summary_en: The Chen family finally took Qi by killing its ruler at Shuzhou (舒州), where Chen Heng had first seized and held him, exactly as Yan Ying had predicted fifty-eight years earlier. Confucius, seventy years old and out of office, purified himself for three days and three times asked his own duke to punish the crime; he was passed from the duke to the great families and got nowhere.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 16 (= -479), immediately after the notice of Confucius's death: 公誄之曰，旻天不弔，不憖遺一老 ... 嗚呼哀哉尼父，無自律 — the duke's eulogy; and Zigong's answer, 生不能用，死而誄之，非禮也。稱一人，非名也。君兩失之 — 'not to use him alive and to eulogise him dead is not ritual; to call yourself "the One Man" is not correct naming; the ruler has failed in both'. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Duke Ai's eulogy over Confucius and Zigong's rebuke
summary_en: The duke lamented over the man he had never employed. Confucius's disciple Zigong said in public that the eulogy was itself a double breach — of ritual, because you do not honour dead a man you would not use alive, and of correct naming, because a duke of Lu is not entitled to call himself 'the One Man'. Both of Confucius's key terms are used against a ruler on the day of the funeral.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 22 (= -473), Chunqiu classic entry and commentary: 冬，十一月，丁卯，越滅吳，請使吳王居甬東。辭曰：「孤老矣，焉能事君？」乃縊，越人以歸 — in winter, in the eleventh month, on the day dingmao, Yue extinguished Wu and offered the king of Wu a residence at Yongdong; he declined, saying 'I am old; how could I serve a lord?', and hanged himself, and the men of Yue took the body home. Duke-year to BCE conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Lu ducal reign years; Zhao 1 = -541, Ding 1 = -509, Ai 1 = -494). Read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08.
title_en: Yue extinguishes Wu and Fuchai hangs himself
summary_en: Twenty-one years after Fuchai spared Goujian on the mountain, Goujian took his capital and offered him a small island to live on. He refused it and hanged himself. Wu Zixu's prediction, made under sentence of death, had come true almost to the year.

dating_basis: Shiji 65, Biographies of Sun Zi and Wu Qi, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 孫子武者，齊人也。以兵法見於吳王闔廬 — 'Master Sun, named Wu, was a man of Qi; he gained an audience with King Helü of Wu on the strength of his art of war'; the chapter ends by crediting him with the breaking of Chu and the entry into Ying. No year is given. The range runs from Helü's accession to the Chu campaign of 506, both of which the Shiji supplies as limits. reliability is LOW because the Zuozhuan, which narrates that campaign year by year, never mentions Sun Wu.
title_en: Sun Wu is presented to King Helü of Wu (traditional)
summary_en: Sima Qian's story: asked to prove his method on the palace women, Sun Wu drilled them, had them laugh at his orders twice, blamed himself the first time and the officers the second, and beheaded the king's two favourite concubines as squad leaders over the king's protest — because a general in the field need not accept even his ruler's command. The near-contemporary annals of the war he is said to have won do not know his name.

dating_basis: Shiji 41, Hereditary House of King Goujian of Yue, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 范蠡事越王句踐，既苦身力，與句踐深謀二十餘年，竟滅吳，報會稽之恥 — Fan Li served King Goujian, wore himself out, planned deeply with him for more than twenty years, and finally destroyed Wu and wiped out the shame of Kuaiji. The range is anchored by the Zuozhuan dates of Kuaiji (Ai 1 = -494) and of the fall of Wu (Ai 22 = -473); the Zuozhuan itself does not name Fan Li, so reliability is medium.
title_en: Fan Li's twenty years rebuilding Yue, and his departure
summary_en: Sima Qian's Fan Li spends twenty years turning a beaten state into the one that destroys Wu, is made supreme general, and then leaves by sea with his jewels and never comes back — writing to his colleague that when the flying birds are gone the good bow is put away, and that Goujian is a man to share hardship with but not ease. The colleague stayed and was given a sword.

dating_basis: Shiji 67, Biographies of the Disciples of Confucius, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 卜商字子夏。少孔子四十四歲 — 'Bu Shang, styled Zixia; forty-four years younger than Confucius.' Confucius's birth is -552/-551 (E_CN_001), so this gives -508/-507. The Shiji gives an interval, not a year; the range is that interval applied to the existing birth range.
title_en: Birth of Zixia
summary_en: Zixia, one of the youngest of the named disciples, is dated only by how much younger he was than his teacher. He outlived Confucius by decades and became, in the tradition, the teacher of the rulers of Wei — the route by which the Confucian classics reached the Warring States courts.

dating_basis: Shiji 67, Biographies of the Disciples of Confucius, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 曾參，南武城人，字子輿。少孔子四十六歲 — 'Zeng Shen, a man of Nan Wucheng, styled Ziyu; forty-six years younger than Confucius.' With Confucius's birth at -552/-551 (E_CN_001) this gives -506/-505. The Shiji gives an interval, not a year.
title_en: Birth of Zengzi
summary_en: Zeng Shen is the disciple the later tradition made its moral centre: the Analects has him examine himself daily on three points, and the classic of filial duty was written in his name centuries after his death.

dating_basis: Shiji 74, the closing notice of the Biographies of Mencius and Xun Qing, read in Chinese at ctext.org 2026-09-08: 墨翟，宋之大夫，善守御，為節用。或曰并孔子時，或曰在其後 — 'Mo Di, a grandee of Song, skilled in defence, advocated frugality. Some say he was contemporary with Confucius, some say he came after him.' That is the whole of the early biographical record and it does not choose between the two datings. The range therefore begins after Confucius's death (-479) with a margin and runs to the end of the century; reliability is low and the width is deliberate. NOT checked against Loewe 1993, which was not reachable this session.
title_en: Mozi and his school are active
summary_en: Somewhere in the century after Confucius, a man from Song began teaching that the world's disorder comes from partial love and that people should care for others' families, houses and states as their own — and organised his followers into disciplined companies that hired themselves out to defend besieged cities. Sima Qian, four centuries later, could not say when he lived.

dating_basis: Zuozhuan, Duke Ai year 14 (= -481). Chunqiu classic entry: 十有四年，春，西狩獲麟 — 'in the fourteenth year, in spring, hunting in the west, a lin was taken'. Zuo narrative: 十四年，春，西狩于大野，叔孫氏之車子鉏商獲麟，以為不祥，以賜虞人。仲尼觀之，曰：「麟也。」然後取之 — the hunt was at Daye; Chu Shang, a carriage-driver of the Shusun family, took the animal, judged it inauspicious and gave it to the game-warden; Zhongni went to look at it and said 'it is a lin', and only then was it taken in. Both lines read in the page source at ctext.org/chun-qiu-zuo-zhuan/ai-gong-shi-si-nian/zh on 2026-09-08. Duke-year conversion per calendars.csv CAL_LU (Ai 1 = -494). ON THE 'END OF THE ANNALS': the Chunqiu entries on this same ctext page continue past the lin into summer, autumn and winter of Ai 14, which is the Zuo recension; the claim that the classic closes here belongs to the Gongyang and Guliang recensions and was NOT verified this session (SRC_GONGYANG and SRC_GULIANG still carry no working url). The summary therefore attributes the association to tradition and asserts nothing about which recension ends where.
title_en: The capture of the lin
summary_en: Hunting in the west at Daye, a driver of the Shusun family caught an animal nobody could name, took it for a bad sign and handed it to the game-warden. Confucius went to look at it and said: it is a lin. Tradition has treated this entry as the sign on which the Spring and Autumn Annals close — the chronicle from which much of this atlas's Chinese material comes.

dating_basis: Herodotus 1.74.2 (Godley, PerseusDL): 'Thales of Miletus had foretold this loss of daylight to the Ionians, fixing it within the year in which the change did indeed happen.' Herodotus gives no calendar year; the identification with the solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BCE is astronomical and is stated in the editorial note printed with the Perseus text at this passage — read 2026-09-08, but NOT independently checked here, which is why reliability is medium rather than high.
title_en: The eclipse Thales foretold ends the war between Lydia and Media
summary_en: Lydians and Medes had fought for five years when, in the middle of a battle, day turned into night. Herodotus says Thales of Miletus had told the Ionians it would happen within the year. Both sides stopped fighting and made peace, sealed by a marriage; the two mediators are named. It is the earliest event in this atlas that anyone claims to have predicted.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.2 (Hicks), citing Apollodorus's Chronology: 'in the second year of the 58th Olympiad Anaximander was sixty-four, and ... he died not long afterwards'. Olympiad conversion per calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD (Ol. n year k = -776 + 4(n-1) + (k-1)). Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy 3rd ed. (chapter The Milesian School, immediately before §13), notes that 547/6 is the year before the fall of Sardis and suggests Apollodorus took the indication from Anaximander's own book. A floruit is stored as an activity range, not a point (conventions §2). The summary's gnomon at Sparta is DL 2.1 (read 2026-10-11, this session): he set it up 'for a sundial in Lacedaemon ... in order to mark the solstices and the equinoxes'.
title_en: Anaximander's sixty-fourth year at Miletus
summary_en: The one dated moment in Anaximander's life. By then he had drawn the first Greek map of the world, set up a gnomon at Sparta to mark the solstices, and written that things arise from and return to a Boundless, paying each other reparation for their injustice by the ordering of time.

dating_basis: Herodotus 1.84-86 narrates the capture of Sardis and the fall of Croesus, and 1.141-176 the subjection of the Ionian and Carian cities that followed, but gives no year. Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy 3rd ed. (chapter The Milesian School), takes 547/6 to be 'just the year before the fall of Sardeis'. The range -547/-545 carries that inference rather than asserting a single year; no permitted source dates the event directly.
title_en: Cyrus takes Sardis; the Ionian cities pass under Persian rule
summary_en: The fall of Lydia put the Greek cities of Asia Minor under a Persian king. For the next fifty years the Ionian philosophers wrote as subjects of an empire, and the revolt that eventually broke out there drew Athens into a war that shaped the fifth century.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 8.3 (Hicks): Pythagoras 'returned to Samos to find his country under the tyranny of Polycrates; so he sailed away to Croton in Italy, and there he laid down a constitution for the Italian Greeks'. DL 8.45 puts his floruit in the 60th Olympiad (= 540-537 BCE); Olympiad conversion per calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD (Ol. n year k = -776 + 4(n-1) + (k-1)). No source gives a year for the voyage, so the range is kept a decade wide.
title_en: Pythagoras leaves Samos for Croton
summary_en: Faced with a tyrant at home, Pythagoras emigrated to southern Italy, where Diogenes says he and about three hundred followers governed Croton so well that its constitution was 'in effect a true aristocracy'. A philosophical school that was also a political party is a new thing in the record.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.18-20 (Hicks): Xenophanes 'was banished from his native city and lived at Zancle in Sicily ... He also lived in Catana', and 'flourished about the 60th Olympiad' (= 540-537 BCE); Olympiad conversion per calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD (Ol. n year k = -776 + 4(n-1) + (k-1)). DL 9.19 quotes his own line that sixty-seven years had been tossing his cares up and down the land of Greece. No year is given for the departure itself; the range begins a little before the floruit.
title_en: Xenophanes is exiled from Colophon and begins a lifetime of wandering
summary_en: Xenophanes left Colophon and spent, on his own account, sixty-seven years moving about Greece, reciting poems that attacked Homer and Hesiod for giving the gods human vices and argued that wisdom deserves the honour cities give to athletes.

dating_basis: Thucydides 6.54-59 (Crawley), who narrates the killing at length precisely to correct the popular Athenian version, and 6.59.4 (MIT plain text, re-read 2026-10-11, this session): 'Hippias, after reigning three years longer over the Athenians, was deposed in the fourth by the Lacedaemonians and the banished Alcmaeonidae'. Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 19 (Kenyon, read the same day) gives a different interval: Hippias began fortifying Munichia 'About three years after the death of Hipparchus' and was expelled while still at the work. Neither gives a calendar year. Counted back from the expulsion in the archon year 511/510 (E_GR_012, anchored on Ath. Pol. 19's archonship of Harpactides and on the Parian Marble's distance from Marathon), Thucydides's 'fourth' year puts the killing three or four archon years earlier and Ath. Pol.'s 'about three years' about three, so the range -515/-513 carries both intervals rather than choosing. The Parian Marble (Ep. 46, 1788 edition, read this session) sets the killing of Hipparchus and the expulsion under one count, 248 years before the stone; Thucydides and Ath. Pol. both separate them by about three years, so that single count is recorded and not used.
title_en: Harmodius and Aristogeiton kill Hipparchus at the Panathenaea
summary_en: Athens remembered the two as tyrannicides who freed the city. Thucydides takes trouble to show that they killed the tyrant's brother, not the tyrant, that the motive was a private love affair, and that the tyranny grew harsher afterwards — his standing example of how badly a city knows its own history.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 19 (Kenyon, MIT plain text, read 2026-10-11, this session): the tyrants surrendered the Acropolis to the Athenians 'in the archonship of Harpactides'. That archon year is the anchor; it is not converted here from the archon list. Its distance from Marathon is read on the Parian Marble (1788 edition, read this session): Ep. 46 counts 248 years since Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus and the Athenians rose to drive the Pisistratidae out of the Pelasgic wall, and Ep. 49 counts 227 since Marathon (both paraphrased from the edition's English and Latin columns), so the stone sets the expulsion 21 archon years before Marathon; with Marathon in 490 (E_GR_017) that is the archon year 511/510. The 1788 edition prints the Ep. 46 archon's name as a bracketed restoration, Cleisthenes, which does not agree with Ath. Pol.'s Harpactides, so the restored name is not used. Thucydides 6.59.4 (Crawley, MIT plain text, re-read the same day) agrees: Hippias was deposed 'by the Lacedaemonians and the banished Alcmaeonidae' and set out from the Persian court 'twenty years after, in his old age, and came with the Medes to Marathon', which with Marathon in 490 gives about 510. Herodotus 5.62-65 gives the narrative of the Spartan intervention and the Delphic pressure behind it.
title_en: Hippias is expelled and the Pisistratid tyranny ends
summary_en: A Spartan army and the exiled Alcmaeonid clan drove out the last tyrant of Athens. Two or three years of factional struggle followed, out of which came Cleisthenes' reorganisation of the citizen body — the event already recorded as E_GR_002.

dating_basis: Herodotus 5.37 (Godley): Aristagoras 'made pretence of giving up his tyranny and gave Miletus equality of government so that the Milesians might readily join in his revolt. Then he proceeded to do the same things in the rest of Ionia.' Herodotus gives no year. The range is fixed at the other end by 6.18, which says Miletus fell 'in the sixth year after the revolt of Aristagoras', so the revolt begins five or six years before the fall of Miletus. The year of that fall, 494 on E_GR_015, is the conventional modern reckoning and is not derived from any source read for this corpus, so this range rests on that convention too.
title_en: Aristagoras gives up his tyranny and the Ionian cities depose their tyrants
summary_en: To make the revolt against Persia popular, the tyrant of Miletus abolished his own office and gave the city isonomia — equality under the law. Herodotus's word here, isonomia, is the one he also gives the Persian Otanes in the debate on constitutions (3.80.6).

dating_basis: Herodotus 5.99-102 (Godley): the Athenians came with twenty ships and the Eretrians with five, the Ionians marched inland from Ephesus, 'they came to Sardis and captured it without any resistance', all but the citadel, and in the fire a temple of Cybebe burnt — 'the Persians afterwards made this their pretext for burning the temples of Hellas'. No year is given; the range follows the six-year span of the revolt (6.18).
title_en: The Ionians and Athenians burn Sardis
summary_en: The one offensive success of the Ionian revolt, and the act Herodotus makes the cause of everything that followed: the burning of a temple at Sardis gave the Persians their justification for burning the temples of Greece, and gave Athens an enemy it kept for two generations.

dating_basis: Herodotus 6.18 (Godley): the Persians 'laid siege to Miletus by sea and land, mining the walls and using every device against it, until they utterly captured it in the sixth year after the revolt of Aristagoras. They enslaved the city.' The interval is the source's; the absolute year 494 is not. It is the conventional modern reckoning, no source read for this corpus fixes it, and the year rests on that convention; E_GR_013's c. 499 is counted back from it. The summary's dead and deported are 6.19.3 ('most of their men were slain by the Persians') and 6.20.1 (the captives brought to Susa and settled 'in the city of Ampe, by which the river Tigris flows as it issues into the sea'), read 2026-10-11, this session.
title_en: Persia destroys Miletus
summary_en: The city of Thales and Anaximander was taken, most of its men killed and its captives settled where the Tigris flows into the sea, and the Ionian revolt ended.

dating_basis: Herodotus 6.21.2 (Godley): 'when Phrynichus wrote a play entitled "The Fall of Miletus" and produced it, the whole theater fell to weeping; they fined Phrynichus a thousand drachmas for bringing to mind a calamity that affected them so personally, and forbade the performance of that play forever.' Herodotus gives no year and places it only after the capture of Miletus; the range runs from that capture (494) to two years later.
title_en: Athens fines Phrynichus for his play on the fall of Miletus
summary_en: The earliest recorded act of theatre censorship: a tragedy about a real and recent disaster made the audience weep, and the city punished the poet for it and banned the play permanently. Herodotus contrasts Athenian grief with the Milesians' own conduct towards Sybaris.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 22 (Kenyon): 'eleven years later, in the archonship of Phaenippus they won the battle of Marathon'. Herodotus 6.100-117 narrates the campaign, including the taking of Eretria (6.101-102) and the casualty figures at 6.117 — 6,400 Persians and 192 Athenians. The absolute year rests on the Athenian archon list (calendars.csv CAL_ARCHON), which was not re-derived here.
title_en: The Persian expedition takes Eretria and is beaten at Marathon
summary_en: Datis and Artaphernes destroyed Eretria and deported its people, then landed at Marathon with the exiled tyrant Hippias to do the same to Athens. The Athenians and Plataeans beat them in the field.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 22 (Kenyon): 'Two years later, in the archonship of Nicodemus, the mines of Maroneia were discovered, and the state made a profit of a hundred talents ... this was prevented by Themistocles', who had a hundred triremes built. Herodotus 7.144 tells the same story with different numbers: the revenue is from the mines at Laurium, the distribution would have been ten drachmas a man, and the ships are two hundred. The two permitted sources disagree, and the range is left four years wide because the archon year is not converted here from the archon list. Ath. Pol. 22 goes on: 'it was with these ships that they fought the battle of Salamis against the barbarians' (re-read 2026-10-11, this session).
title_en: Athens spends the silver strike on a fleet instead of dividing it
summary_en: A windfall from the state silver mines was about to be shared out among the citizens when Themistocles persuaded the assembly to build warships with it instead. Aristotle's Constitution adds that these were the ships with which Athens fought at Salamis.

dating_basis: Herodotus 8.51.1 (Godley) dates Xerxes' arrival in Attica in the same campaign 'when Calliades was archon at Athens', four months after the crossing of the Hellespont; the stand at Thermopylae is narrated at 7.201-233, earlier in the same march. The archon year 480/479 is the standard equivalence for Calliades (calendars.csv CAL_ARCHON) and was not re-derived here.
title_en: The Greek stand at Thermopylae
summary_en: Leonidas and his allies held the pass from Thessaly into central Greece until a local man showed the Persians a path around it.

dating_basis: Herodotus 8.51.1 (Godley): 'Since the crossing of the Hellespont ... they had spent one month there crossing into Europe and in three more months were in Attica, when Calliades was archon at Athens.' 8.53 describes the climb up the unguarded cliff by the precinct of Aglaurus and the taking of the acropolis. Archon year per calendars.csv CAL_ARCHON.
title_en: Xerxes takes and burns Athens
summary_en: The city was evacuated and the Persians took the acropolis by climbing a cliff nobody guarded.

dating_basis: Herodotus 8.83-96 (Godley) narrates the battle in the strait; 8.95 has Aristides land hoplites on the islet of Psyttalea in the middle of it (8.95.1 re-read 2026-10-11, this session: 'they slaughtered all the Persians who were on that islet'). The year follows the archonship of Calliades given at 8.51.1 for the same campaign (calendars.csv CAL_ARCHON).
title_en: The sea battle at Salamis
summary_en: The Greek fleet fought in the narrows off Salamis, where the Persian numbers could not be brought to bear, and won. In the confusion Aristides landed armed men on the islet of Psyttalea, and they killed all the Persians on it.

dating_basis: Herodotus 9.59-70 (Godley) narrates the battle and gives the Greek dead at 9.70.5: 91 Lacedaemonians from Sparta, 52 Athenians, and Tegeans numbered differently in the two digital files of the same edition, both re-read 2026-10-11, this session: the Greek (perseus-grc2) reads Τεγεητέων δὲ ἑκκαίδεκα, sixteen, and the English (perseus-eng2) 'of the Tegeans, seventeen'. Both readings are recorded and neither is chosen; a page image of Godley's printed Loeb was not seen. The year is the one after Salamis on Herodotus's own sequence of summers; Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25 later counts 'about seventeen years after the Persian wars' to the archonship of Conon, which is consistent with 479 as the end of the wars.
title_en: The Greeks defeat the Persian army at Plataea
summary_en: The last land battle of the invasion. Herodotus counts the Greek dead city by city: ninety-one Spartans, fifty-two Athenians, and sixteen or seventeen Tegeans, for the Greek text and its English translation disagree on that number.

dating_basis: Thucydides 1.96 (Crawley): the Athenians 'fixed which cities were to contribute money against the barbarian, which ships ... Now was the time that the office of "Treasurers for Hellas" was first instituted by the Athenians ... The tribute was first fixed at four hundred and sixty talents. The common treasury was at Delos, and the congresses were held in the temple.' Thucydides gives no year; the range follows immediately on his narrative of the Hellespont campaign and the recall of Pausanias at 1.94-95.
title_en: The Delian League is founded and its treasury placed on Delos
summary_en: An alliance of free cities against Persia, with a common congress in the temple of Apollo, an assessed contribution and Athenian treasurers. Within a generation the treasury had moved to Athens and the contribution had become tribute; Thucydides tells the story as the birth of an empire that nobody voted for.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25 (Kenyon): 'The supremacy of the Areopagus lasted for about seventeen years after the Persian wars ... Then, in the archonship of Conon, he stripped the Council of all the acquired prerogatives from which it derived its guardianship of the constitution, and assigned some of them to the Council of Five Hundred, and others to the Assembly and the law-courts.' Seventeen years from 479 gives about 462; the range carries the word 'about' and the fact that the archon year was not converted here from the archon list.
title_en: Ephialtes strips the Areopagus of its guardianship of the constitution
summary_en: The old aristocratic council lost its power to supervise magistrates and annul decisions; the powers went to the Council of Five Hundred, the Assembly and the popular juries. It is the moment Athenian democracy stops sharing authority with a body nobody elected.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 25 (Kenyon): 'Not long afterwards, however, Ephialtes was assassinated by Aristodicus of Tanagra.' No year is given; the range runs from the start of the reform's own range on E_GR_024 (-463) and carries the vagueness of 'not long afterwards'.
title_en: Ephialtes is assassinated
summary_en: The author of the reform was murdered within a few years of carrying it, by a man from Tanagra. The reform stood; Pericles took over the leadership of the people.

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 26 (Kenyon): 'two years afterwards, in the archonship of Antidotus, [in] consequence of the great increase in the number of citizens, it was resolved, on the motion of Pericles, that no one should [be] admitted to the franchise who was not of citizen birth by both parents.' Ath. Pol. dates it only by archon and by intervals from the death of Ephialtes (five years to Mnesitheides, four more to Lysicrates, two more to Antidotus). The absolute year 451/450 rests on the archon list, which was not consulted here, so the range is left three years wide.
title_en: Pericles' citizenship law: both parents must be Athenian
summary_en: At the height of Athenian openness the assembly narrowed citizenship to the children of two Athenian parents. The city that invented political equality also invented a strict definition of who was inside it.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 2.12-14 (Hicks) gives three incompatible accounts: Sotion says he was indicted by Cleon for impiety 'because he declared the sun to be a mass of red-hot metal', defended by Pericles, fined five talents and banished; Satyrus says the prosecutor was Thucydides son of Melesias, the charge included medism, and sentence of death was passed in absence; Hieronymus says Pericles brought him into court so ill that he was acquitted out of pity. No source gives a year. DL 2.7 (re-read 2026-10-11, this session) says he began philosophy at Athens 'in the archonship of Callias when he was twenty', that he was twenty at the invasion of Xerxes, and that 'at Athens they say he remained for thirty years'. Born in the 70th Olympiad (-500/-497, P_ANAXAGORAS), he was twenty in -480/-477, and the invasion of Xerxes is 480 in this corpus (E_GR_020); the archonship of Callias is not converted here from the archon list. The range runs from the start of his Athenian period (-480) to his death in the first year of the 88th Olympiad (428/427, DL 2.7), between which the trial must fall. The thirty years would end his stay about -450/-447, but Diogenes does not tie the trial to the end of the stay, so that figure is recorded and not used as a bound. Reliability low because the sources contradict each other on the outcome.
title_en: Anaxagoras is prosecuted at Athens for impiety
summary_en: The first recorded trial of a philosopher for what he taught about the natural world: that the sun is a red-hot stone and not a god. Diogenes preserves three versions with three different verdicts, which is a fair measure of what is actually known about it.

dating_basis: Diogenes Laertius 9.50 (Hicks), citing Heraclides of Pontus On Laws, says Protagoras 'was born at Abdera ... and also that he made laws for Thurii'. DL 9.56 puts his floruit in the 84th Olympiad (= 444-441 BCE); Olympiad conversion per calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD (Ol. n year k = -776 + 4(n-1) + (k-1)). No source dates the lawgiving itself, so the range is the floruit.
title_en: Protagoras writes laws for the new colony at Thurii
summary_en: A man who taught that there are two sides to every question and that the human being is the measure of all things was asked to write the constitution of a new panhellenic city in Italy. It is the clearest case in the record of sophistic argument being trusted with public business.

dating_basis: Thucydides 2.2.1 (Crawley): 'in the fifteenth [year of the truce], in the forty-eighth year of the priestess-ship of Chrysis at Argos, in the Ephorate of Aenesias at Sparta, in the last month but two of the Archonship of Pythodorus at Athens, and six months after the battle of Potidaea, just at the beginning of spring, a Theban force ... made an armed entry into Plataea.' Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 27 independently dates the outbreak 'forty-eight years after the battle of Salamis, in the archonship of Pythodorus'. Two permitted sources, one archon.
title_en: The Theban attack on Plataea begins the Peloponnesian War
summary_en: Thucydides dates the opening of the war four different ways at once — by an Argive priestess, a Spartan ephor, an Athenian archon and an interval — because Greece had no common calendar. The twenty-seven years that followed produced the plague, the Melian dialogue, the Sicilian disaster and, at the end of them, the trial of Socrates.

dating_basis: Thucydides 2.65.6 (Crawley): 'He outlived its commencement two years and six months' — the commencement being the spring of 431 dated at 2.2.1 — which places his death in the autumn of 429. CORRECTED AT A2, 2026-09-08: Thucydides does NOT give a cause of death. 2.65.6 supplies only the interval; the plague is everywhere in the surrounding narrative (2.61.3; 2.64.1, where Pericles calls it 'the only point indeed at which our calculation has been at fault') but is nowhere connected to his death. The A1 row titled this 'Pericles dies in the plague at Athens', which the cited source does not support. The attribution of his death to the plague comes from Plutarch, Pericles 38 — admitted as a source by ruling L-30 but NOT read this session, so it is not cited. The epidemic is now its own event, E_GR_041.
title_en: Death of Pericles
summary_en: Thucydides marks his death by an interval — two years and six months after the war began — and by the remark that his foresight was better understood once he was gone. He had spent his last months defending his own strategy to a city that had turned on him, telling the assembly that the epidemic was the one thing his calculation had not allowed for.

dating_basis: Thucydides 3.36-49 (Crawley), placed in his narrative in the summer following the second year of the plague: the Athenians 'in the fury of the moment determined to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens, but the whole adult male population of Mitylene' (3.36.2), repented overnight, debated again, and sent a second ship that arrived 'so little before' the first that the massacre was prevented (3.49.4). The absolute year follows Thucydides' count of summers and winters from the spring of 431.
title_en: Athens votes to kill the men of Mytilene, then votes again
summary_en: A decree of collective execution was passed, regretted and reversed in a single day, and a second trireme rowed all night to overtake the first. Cleon argued that an empire is a tyranny and must be feared; Diodotus argued not from mercy but from what would actually work. The debate is the first surviving argument about deterrence.

dating_basis: Thucydides 5.84-116 (Crawley), in the summer before the Sicilian expedition of 415: the conference of envoys is at 5.85-113 and the outcome at 5.116.4 — the Melians 'surrendered at discretion to the Athenians, who put to death all the grown men whom they took, and sold the women and children for slaves, and subsequently sent out five hundred colonists'. The absolute year follows Thucydides' count of summers and winters.
title_en: The Melian dialogue and the destruction of Melos
summary_en: Athenian envoys told the magistrates of a small neutral island that questions of right arise only between equals in power, and that the strong do what they can while the weak suffer what they must. Melos refused, was besieged, and its men were killed and its women and children sold. Thucydides admits he reconstructed the speeches, which is why reliability here is medium.

dating_basis: Thucydides 6.53.1 and 6.61.4 (Crawley): while the fleet was at Catana 'they found the Salaminia come from Athens for Alcibiades, with orders for him to sail home to answer the charges which the state brought against him ... of sacrilege in the matter of the mysteries and of the Hermae'; 6.61.4 says 'it was therefore decided to bring him to trial and execute him'. The year follows Thucydides' narrative sequence from the sailing of the expedition (6.30-32). The summary's going over to Sparta is 6.61.6-7 (he leaves the Salaminia at Thurii and, 'now an outlaw, crossed in a boat not long after from Thurii to Peloponnese') and 6.88.9 (the Corinthian envoys find him at Lacedaemon, where he had come at the Lacedaemonians' own invitation), read 2026-10-11, this session.
title_en: The mutilation of the Herms and the recall of Alcibiades for trial
summary_en: On the eve of the greatest expedition Athens ever sent out, the stone Herms all over the city were found defaced overnight. In the panic Alcibiades was accused of profaning the mysteries and recalled from his own command; he went over to Sparta instead. Religion, rumour and politics in one episode.

dating_basis: Thucydides 6.8-7.87 (Crawley). The expedition sails in the summer after the Egestaean envoys arrive with sixty talents (6.8.1); it ends at 7.87.5, 'the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in this war, or, in my opinion, in Hellenic history; at once most glorious to the victors, and most calamitous to the conquered'. The absolute years follow Thucydides' count of summers and winters from 431.
title_en: The Athenian expedition to Sicily and its destruction at Syracuse
summary_en: Athens sent the largest force ever raised by a Greek city against a city it barely knew, on the advice of a man it recalled for trial before he arrived. Two fleets and two armies were lost. Thucydides makes the whole affair turn on a crowd's appetite for an enterprise nobody had examined.

dating_basis: Thucydides 8.65-70 (Crawley, in the PerseusDL eng6 copy, SRC_CRAWLEY_THUC_BK8, because the MIT text stops at 8.7; 8.68.1-4 and 8.70.1 re-read there 2026-10-11, this session): the motion was moved by Pisander, and 'the Four Hundred entered the council chamber ... but afterwards departed widely from the democratic system of government ... and ruled the city by force' (8.70.1). Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 29-33 gives the constitutional documents and names Melobius and Pythodorus of Anaphlystus. The year follows Thucydides' sequence after the Sicilian disaster.
title_en: The Four Hundred overthrow the Athenian democracy
summary_en: Under the pressure of defeat, an assembly voted its own constitution away. Thucydides names the men who managed it — Pisander in front, Antiphon behind, with Phrynichus and Theramenes — and remarks how hard a thing it was to do to a people that had been free for nearly a hundred years.

dating_basis: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.7 (read at PerseusDL 2026-09-08): the assembly rejected Euryptolemus's motion to try the generals one by one under the decree of Cannonus and voted the Senate's motion to judge them all together; 'after this they condemned the generals who took part in the battle, eight in all; and the six who were in Athens were put to death' (1.7.34). Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 34 dates the battle of Arginusae to 'the archonship of Callias of Angele', six years after the overthrow of the Four Hundred. The archon year is not converted here from the archon list; six years from 411 gives 406.
title_en: Athens condemns the generals of Arginusae in a single vote
summary_en: After a naval victory in which men were left to drown in a storm, the assembly tried the eight generals together in one vote, against the law and against the objection of the presiding councillors — one of whom, Xenophon says elsewhere, was Socrates. Six were executed. Athens regretted it almost at once.

dating_basis: Xenophon, Hellenica 2.2.23 (read at PerseusDL 2026-09-08): 'After this Lysander sailed into Piraeus, the exiles returned, and the Peloponnesians with great enthusiasm began to tear down the walls to the music of flute-girls, thinking that that day was the beginning of freedom for Greece.' Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 34 places the surrender in the year after the archonship of Callias. The absolute year rests on the archon list, not re-derived here.
title_en: Athens surrenders and the Long Walls are pulled down
summary_en: The terms of peace destroyed the fleet, the walls and the empire. Xenophon's flute-girls playing while the walls came down is one of the few images in his history that everyone remembers.

dating_basis: Xenophon, Hellenica 2.3.11 (read at PerseusDL 2026-09-08): 'the Thirty had been chosen as soon as the long walls and the walls round Piraeus were demolished; although chosen ... for the purpose of framing a constitution ... they continually delayed'. Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 35: 'In this way were the Thirty established in power, in the archonship of Pythodorus', and 34 records that the assembly was intimidated into voting the oligarchy on the motion of Dracontides. Archon year not converted here from the archon list.
title_en: The Thirty rule Athens
summary_en: A commission appointed to write a constitution governed instead by executions and confiscations, with a Spartan garrison. Aristotle notes that they began by taking down the laws of Ephialtes from the Areopagus hill. Socrates, who refused one of their orders, was tried four years after they fell, by the democracy they had discredited. Plato, Apology 32 (Fowler, read 2026-09-08) has him describe the order: 'the Thirty sent for me with four others to come to the rotunda and ordered us to bring Leon the Salaminian from Salamis to be put to death. They gave many such orders to others also, because they wished to implicate as many in their crimes as they could.'

dating_basis: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 39 (Kenyon): 'This reconciliation was effected in the archonship of Eucleides', and the terms follow. Xenophon, Hellenica 2.4.43 (read at PerseusDL 2026-09-08): the two parties, 'pledged as they were under oath, that in very truth they would not remember past grievances ... even to this day live together as fellow-citizens and the commons abide by their oaths.' Archon year not converted here from the archon list.
title_en: The democracy is restored and Athens swears not to remember
summary_en: After the Thirty fell, the returning democrats swore an oath of amnesty — literally, of not recalling past wrongs — and, Xenophon says with evident surprise, kept it. It is the legal setting of the trial of Socrates a few years later.

dating_basis: Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.2 (read at PerseusDL 2026-09-08): 'As to how Cyrus collected an army and with this army made the march up country against his brother, how the battle was fought, how Cyrus was slain, and how after that the Greeks effected their return in safety to the sea — all this has been written by Themistogenes the Syracusan.' Xenophon gives no year here; the campaign falls between the restoration of the Athenian democracy (403) and the Spartan campaigns in Asia with which Hellenica book 3 continues. The summary's generals and Xenophon rest on Anabasis 2.5.31-32 (the generals seized at Tissaphernes' doors), 2.6.1 and 3.1.47 ('Xenophon the Athenian in place of Proxenus'), Brownson, PerseusDL perseus-eng2, read 2026-10-11, this session; Hellenica 3.1.2 was re-read the same day.
title_en: The march of the Ten Thousand into Persia and back
summary_en: Greek mercenaries marched inland with Cyrus against his brother the king; Cyrus was killed in the battle, and the Greeks made their way back to the sea. In the Anabasis, the account of the march, the army's generals are seized and it chooses new ones, among them Xenophon the Athenian; Xenophon's own Hellenica credits the account of the march to Themistogenes the Syracusan.

dating_basis: Thucydides 2.47.3 (Crawley): 'Not many days after their arrival in Attica the plague first began to show itself among the Athenians' — the arrival being the second Peloponnesian invasion, which his count of summers and winters from the spring of 431 (2.2.1) places in 430. 2.54.5 closes the first account: 'Such was the history of the plague.' 3.87.1-2 records the return: 'The winter following, the plague a second time attacked the Athenians ... The second visit lasted no less than a year, the first having lasted two.' Two years from 430, an abatement, then a further year gives a span running to about 426. Thucydides dates by summers and winters and never by a calendar year, so the range carries that and no single year is asserted. The summary's two further claims are 2.48.3 ('as I had the disease myself') and 3.87.3 ('No less than four thousand four hundred heavy infantry in the ranks died of it and three hundred cavalry'), read 2026-10-11, this session, in the MIT text.
title_en: The plague at Athens
summary_en: An epidemic reached Athens in the second summer of the war, ran for two years, abated, and came back for a third. Thucydides caught it himself and watched it in others; he refused to speculate about its causes and set down the symptoms instead, so that it could be recognised if it ever returned. He counted 4,400 hoplites and 300 cavalry dead in the ranks alone, and said nothing reduced Athenian power more.

dating_basis: Ezekiel 8:1, read at its locator this session: the sixth year, the sixth month, the fifth day of the month. Ezekiel dates by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity (Ezekiel 1:2, read this session). The captivity begins with the deportation the Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 Rev. 11-13 fixes to the second of Addaru in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year (February/March 597), re-read at livius.org this session. Counting Babylonian years from Nisan, a stamp in months 1-9 of captivity-year N falls in the Julian year 598 minus N, and a stamp in months 10-12 falls in 597 minus N. That conversion is applied openly on every Ezekiel row in this batch, and where the month is not given the row carries the two-year range the ambiguity produces. Month 6 of year 6 gives 592.
title_en: Ezekiel is carried in vision from Babylonia into the Temple
summary_en: Sitting in his own house among the exiles with the elders of Judah before him, Ezekiel is taken in vision to Jerusalem and shown what is being done inside the Temple. Place note: the exact settlement (Tel-abib on the Chebar canal) is not securely located, so Babylon stands as the region's proxy point, as on E_IL_002.

Ezekiel dates by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity (Ezekiel 1:2, read this session). title_en: The elders of Israel come to Ezekiel to inquire of the LORD
summary_en: Elders of the exiled community sit down before the prophet to ask for an oracle, and are given instead a history of their own people's rebellion - the speech in which the sabbath is named as the sign between God and Israel (20:12).

dating_basis: 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4, both read at their locators this session: the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, the tenth month, the tenth day of the month. Zedekiah's accession is the deportation of 597 (ABC 5 Rev. 11-13), so his ninth year runs from spring 589; a tenth-month date falls at the turn into 588, which is why the range spans two Julian years rather than asserting one.
title_en: Nebuchadnezzar encamps against Jerusalem and the siege begins
summary_en: The king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem, encamped against it and built forts against it round about. The siege lasted into Zedekiah's eleventh year, when the famine in the city became severe and the wall was breached.

dating_basis: Ezekiel 24:1-2, read at its locator this session: the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day of the month. Ezekiel dates by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity (Ezekiel 1:2, read this session). title_en: Subhadda, the last person the Buddha admits
summary_en: A wanderer hears that the ascetic Gotama will be extinguished in the last watch of the night and comes with a question: did all those famous teachers really have direct knowledge, or none of them, or only some? He is told to let that be, and given instead the test that wherever the eightfold path is not found, no true ascetic is found. It is in answering him that the Buddha gives his own age at going forth.

title_en: The last words, and what is to count as the teacher afterwards
summary_en: He tells them not to think the teacher's dispensation has passed and that they have no teacher: the teaching and the training that I have taught and pointed out for you shall be your Teacher after my passing. He allows the order to abolish the lesser rules if it wishes, asks three times whether anyone has a doubt to raise, gets silence, and says: conditions fall apart, persist with diligence.

summary_en: The Mallas spend six days honouring the body with dance, song, music, garlands and awnings, and cremate it on the seventh. Ananda tells them to proceed as for the corpse of a wheel-turning monarch and to build a monument at the crossroads: the funeral of a king, for a man who refused to be one.

title_en: The relics are divided into eight portions
summary_en: Ajatasattu of Magadha, the Licchavis of Vesali, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, the Bulis of Allakappa, the Koliyans of Ramagama, the brahmin of Vethadipa and the Mallas of Pava all send for a share; the Mallas of Kusinara refuse. The brahmin Dona stops the quarrel by proposing eight portions, so that there may be monuments far and wide. Whatever else it is, it is a list of the powers of the eastern Ganges plain in one generation.

summary_en: Travelling with five hundred monks he sits down under a tree, sees an Ajivaka coming the other way carrying a coral-tree flower, and asks whether he knows anything about our teacher. Today it is seven days since the ascetic Gotama attained final extinguishment; that is why I carry this flower. No place is recorded, because the segment names a road and not a village.
