title_en: The first communal recitation is proposed
summary_en: An old monk in the travelling party says out loud that it is good to be free of the great ascetic, who was forever telling them what was allowable and what was not; now they can do as they like. Mahakassapa's answer to that is to propose that the teaching and the discipline be recited together and fixed before anything else is lost.

year_display: within the Buddha's teaching life, c. 471-380 BCE (short chronology)
dating_basis: No source read in this session dates this by a calendar year; the Pali canon dates nothing that way. The range is the Buddha's teaching life on the corpus's own frame: DN 16:5.27.5-8 has him say he went forth at twenty-nine and that it is over fifty years since, and DN 16:2.25.10 has him say he is eighty years old; P_BUDDHA carries the short chronology (Bechert), birth -500/-460 and death -420/-380. Going-forth is therefore about 471 at the earliest and the death about 380 at the latest, and that whole span is the range here because the sources place this event inside the teaching life and nowhere more exactly. reliability=low says exactly that. pli-tv-kd1:6.1-6.4, read at its locator this session.
title_en: The two teachers who died too soon to hear it
summary_en: Before going to the five, the Buddha thinks of his own former teachers - Alara Kalama, and then Udaka Ramaputta - and is told that one died seven days ago and the other last night. The first thing the tradition records him doing after deciding to teach is discovering that the people he wanted to tell are dead.

year_display: c. 460-445 BCE (a scene in Plato, not a dated event)
dating_basis: Plato, Parmenides 127b-c (Fowler, PerseusDL), read at its locator this session: Zeno and Parmenides once came to the Great Panathenaea; Parmenides was already quite elderly, about sixty-five years old, very white-haired; Zeno was about forty; and Socrates was then very young. THE SOURCE GIVES NO YEAR, and the Panathenaic festival recurred, so the range here is derived only from what this corpus already holds: P_SOCRATES's birth range (-470/-469) plus an interpretation of very young as somewhere between about ten and twenty-five years old. That interpretation is mine and is disclosed as one. reliability=low, and the summary says in the reader's hearing that this is a scene Plato wrote two generations later.
title_en: Parmenides and Zeno come to Athens, and a very young Socrates hears them
summary_en: Plato opens his hardest dialogue with a meeting he places long before his own lifetime: the old Eleatic, white-haired and about sixty-five, his pupil Zeno of forty reading his treatises aloud in Athens for the first time, and a boy called Socrates listening to the end and then asking for the first argument again. It is a scene by a later writer, not a report; it is recorded here because it is the only thing a permitted source read in this session puts a number on for Parmenides.

dating_basis: Three passages of the Histories read at their locators this session in the PerseusDL Godley file. 7.137: the wrath of Talthybius rose up again in the war between the Peloponnesians and Athenians, and the sons of the Spartan envoys were put to death by the Athenians - so the war has begun and this episode has happened. 9.73: even as recently as the war waged many years after this time between the Athenians and Peloponnesians, the Lacedaemonians laid no hand on Decelea when they harried the rest of Attica - the annual invasions, not the permanent occupation. 6.98: in three generations, in the time of Darius, Xerxes and Artaxerxes, more ills came on Greece than in twenty generations before Darius. The lower bound is the outbreak of the war (E_GR_029, spring 431); the upper bound follows the composition range already carried by W_HERODOTUS and is the softer of the two. CAUTION: the Perseus English file interleaves editorial notes with the text, and the modern dates that appear at 7.137 and 9.73 are Perseus's, not Herodotus's; none of them is used here.
title_en: Herodotus is at work: the Histories reach into the Peloponnesian War
summary_en: The first prose history of the world is still being written while the war that ends its world is going on. The book keeps glancing forward out of its own subject - to Spartan envoys' sons killed by Athens, to Attica being harried, to three generations of Persian kings - and those glances are what date it. This row is the compositional window; P_HERODOTUS still carries no birth or death year, because no source read in this session gives one.

dating_basis: Nabonidus Chronicle ii 1-4 (livius.org, read 2026-09-13): in Nabonidus's sixth year Astyages marched against Cyrus king of Anšan, his army rebelled and handed him over, and Cyrus marched to Ecbatana, the royal city, and carried its silver and gold to Anšan. The Julian years are re-derived, not taken from the page's gloss: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 11 (read this session) has Nabonidus's 17th year end with the fall of Babylon in October 539, so his 6th year runs from Nisanu 550 to Nisanu 549, and the range carries both Julian years. Herodotus 1.127-130 (read this session) narrates the desertion and capture and gives no year.
title_en: Cyrus defeats Astyages and takes Ecbatana
summary_en: The Median king marched against his Persian vassal and his own army mutinied and handed him over. Cyrus then entered the Median royal city and carried off its treasure. From this point the Persians rule the Medes, not the other way round.

dating_basis: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12 (read 2026-09-13): the last Babylonian tablets dated to Cyrus are of July-August 530 and Cambyses is sole king by 31 August 530; Cyrus's death on the north-eastern front was probably reported in Babylon in August. Herodotus 1.214 (read this session) has Cyrus fall fighting the Massagetae under queen Tomyris 'after having reigned for one year short of thirty years', and says in the same chapter that many stories of his death are told. The year rests on the tablets; the manner of death on Herodotus alone, hence reliability=medium.
title_en: Cyrus dies on campaign in the east
summary_en: The founder of the empire died on a campaign beyond its north-eastern frontier. Herodotus tells of a battle against the Massagetae and a queen who dipped his head in blood, and admits it is one story among many. Babylonian scribes started dating documents by his son Cambyses.

dating_basis: Diodorus 1.68.6 (Loeb vol. I, 1933, via LacusCurtius, read 2026-09-13): the Egyptian king Amasis died when Cambyses attacked Egypt, in the third year of the 63rd Olympiad; Ol. 63.3 = 526/525 by calendars.csv CAL_OLYMPIAD. Herodotus 3.13-15 (read this session) narrates the rout, the siege and surrender of Memphis and the capture of Psammenitus after a six-month reign, and gives no year. Cambyses's reign in Babylonia, 530-522 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12, read this session), brackets it. reliability=medium: the synchronism is Diodorus's, four centuries later.
title_en: Cambyses conquers Egypt
summary_en: The Persian army routed the Egyptians, besieged Memphis until it surrendered, and took the young king Psammenitus prisoner. Libya and Cyrene sent tribute without fighting. Egypt became a Persian province and stayed one, with revolts, for most of two centuries.

dating_basis: Behistun col. I §11 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13): the Magian Gaumata rose up when 14 days of Viyakhna were completing their course and seized the kingdom when 9 days of Garmapada were; Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12 (read this session) converts these to 11 March and 1 July 522, and records tablets dated to Bardiya in Babylonia from April 522.
title_en: The Magian Gaumata seizes the throne as 'Bardiya son of Cyrus'
summary_en: While Cambyses was away, a man claiming to be his brother Bardiya was accepted as king in Persia, Media and the other provinces, and Babylonian scribes dated documents by him. Darius, who later killed him, says he was a Magian named Gaumata and an impostor; that account is the only near-contemporary one there is.

dating_basis: Behistun col. I §11 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13): after Gaumata seized the kingdom 'Cambyses died by a self-imposed death'; Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12 (read this session): Cambyses still recognised in Babylonia in April 522, and Behistun §11 implies he died after 1 July 522. Herodotus 3.64-66 (read this session): wounded in the thigh by his own sword at Ecbatana in Syria, dead about twenty days later, having reigned seven years and five months.
title_en: Cambyses dies on the way home from Egypt
summary_en: Hearing that a usurper ruled in his brother's name, Cambyses set out for home and died on the road. Darius's inscription says his death was self-inflicted; Herodotus says his own sword cut him as he mounted his horse.

dating_basis: Herodotus 3.80-83 (read 2026-09-13): the council was held 'after the tumult quieted down, and five days passed' from the killing of the Magi, which Behistun col. I §13 and Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12 (both read this session) date to 29 September 522 (E_PE_002). Herodotus insists the speeches were really made though some Greeks disbelieve it (3.80.1, repeated at 6.43.3, read this session). No Persian source mentions a debate, hence reliability=low. Place left blank: Herodotus sets the plot at Susa (3.70.3), Behistun sets the killing in Media (col. I §13).
title_en: Seven Persian nobles debate democracy, oligarchy and monarchy
summary_en: In Herodotus's account the conspirators, before choosing a king, argued about whether to have one. Otanes spoke for rule by the people, with offices by lot and power held to account; another spoke for rule by the best few; Darius argued that one excellent man rules best, and four of seven agreed. It is the earliest surviving comparison of the three kinds of constitution, written by a Greek and set in Persia.

dating_basis: Herodotus 3.84-88 (read 2026-09-13) narrates the contest directly after the debate (E_PE_009) and before Darius's first acts as king; the year follows E_PE_002 (Behistun col. I §13; Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 12, both read this session). Herodotus himself gives two versions of the groom's trick; no other source read tells the story, hence reliability=low.
title_en: Darius becomes king when his horse neighs first
summary_en: The conspirators agreed that the kingship would go to the man whose horse neighed first at sunrise. Darius's groom made sure it was his, and thunder and lightning out of a clear sky were taken as the sign that settled it. Herodotus tells it as a story, with two versions of the trick.

dating_basis: Behistun col. I §§18-19 and col. II §1 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13): Darius crossed the Tigris and defeated Nidintu-Bel, who called himself Nebuchadrezzar, on the 26th of Athriyadiya, fought again at Zazana, then seized Babylon and slew Nidintu-Bel there. Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 13 (read this session) converts the two battles to 13 and 18 December 522 and says Darius captured and killed him 'shortly thereafter'; Darius's first secure Babylonian tablets are of January-February 521. The range allows the capture to fall in either year.
title_en: Darius defeats Nidintu-Bel and retakes Babylon
summary_en: Babylon had declared for a man claiming to be a son of its last native king. Darius crossed the Tigris with his army on skin floats and camels, won two battles, took the city and executed the pretender there. It is the first of the rebellions Darius lists.

dating_basis: Behistun col. II §5 and §13 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13): Phraortes rose up in Media claiming to be of the family of Cyaxares; he was taken at Raga, brought to Darius, mutilated, held bound at court and put on a cross at Ecbatana. No year stands in the paragraphs; Behistun col. IV §2 (read this session) places the rebellions 'in the same year after that I became king', which Tolman's own note says is disputed. The range therefore runs from the accession (late 522) through 521, and reliability is medium.
title_en: Darius captures the Median rebel Phraortes and crucifies him at Ecbatana
summary_en: A Mede claiming the old Median royal line took the palace and most of Media. Darius's generals broke his army; he fled to Raga and was brought back, disfigured, kept in chains where everyone could see him, and put on a cross in the Median capital with his chief supporters.

dating_basis: Behistun col. III §§14-15 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13): Arkha, an Armenian who called himself Nebuchadrezzar son of Nabonidus, seized Babylon; Intaphernes defeated the Babylonians and Arkha and his chief allies were put on the cross at Babylon. Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 13-14 (read this session): tablets dated to 'Nebuchadnezzar IV' run from September to November 521, and his capture, citing Behistun §§49-50, fell on 27 November 521.
title_en: Babylon rebels a second time and the pretender Arkha is crucified
summary_en: While Darius was in Persia and Media, Babylon went over to another man claiming to be the son of its last king. Darius's general Intaphernes retook the city; the pretender and his chief men were put on crosses there. Babylonian scribes had dated contracts by the rebel for about two months.

dating_basis: Herodotus 3.89 (read 2026-09-13) tells the reform directly after Darius's accession and marriages but gives no year. The range is Darius's reign as Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 13-14 (read this session) fixes it. A 36-year range, so reliability cannot be high; medium because the fact of a fixed tribute is reported plainly and the date only by position in the narrative.
title_en: Darius divides the empire into twenty satrapies and fixes their tribute
summary_en: Under Cyrus and Cambyses the provinces had sent gifts; Darius set each one a fixed annual payment in silver or gold and grouped the peoples into twenty governorships. Herodotus says this is why the Persians called Darius the merchant, Cambyses the master and Cyrus the father.

dating_basis: Herodotus 4.44 (read 2026-09-13) gives no year. Lower bound: the list of 23 countries in Behistun col. I §6 (Tolman 1908, read this session; W_BEHISTUN -520/-518) does not include India, while Darius's later lists do (Persepolis e §2 and Naqsh-i Rustam a §3, both read this session). Upper bound: Darius's death, November 486 (Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 14). reliability=medium.
title_en: Scylax sails down the Indus to the sea, and Darius adds India to the empire
summary_en: Wanting to know where the Indus reached the sea, Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda and others down the river and around by sea; they arrived in the Red Sea in the thirtieth month. Herodotus says Darius then subdued the Indians. India appears in Darius's later lists of provinces, not in the Behistun list.

year_display: between Darius's accession and the Ionian revolt
dating_basis: Herodotus 4.83-98 (read at 4.87, 4.89, 4.97 on 2026-09-13) gives no year. The range is the narrative's own frame: after Darius's accession (E_PE_002, 522) and before the Ionian revolt, which the merged E_GR_013 dates c. 499 from Herodotus 5.37 and 6.18. The Scythian campaign in Behistun col. V §4 (read this session) is against Asian Scythians and is not treated as the same war. reliability=low. The order and its reversal: 4.97.1-6 and 4.98.1-3 (re-read 2026-10-13): Darius has the Ionians break the bridge, accepts Coes's advice, and tells them 'I take back the decision which I delivered before about the bridge' and to 'guard the bridge'.
title_en: Darius bridges the Bosporus and marches against the Scythians of Europe
summary_en: Darius had Mandrocles of Samos build a bridge of ships across the Bosporus, set up pillars listing the nations in his army, and crossed into Europe, while Ionian Greeks bridged the Danube for him. On reaching the Danube he ordered the Ionians to break up that bridge and follow him across the mainland, then, on the advice of Coes of Mytilene, took back the order and set them to guard it.

dating_basis: Suez stela c §3 (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13) records the canal in Darius's first person but carries no date; the range is his reign per Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 13-14 (read this session). reliability=medium: the text is Darius's own, the date is only its bracket.
title_en: Darius has a canal dug from the Nile to the sea
summary_en: On stelae set up along its course Darius declared: I am a Persian; from Persia I seized Egypt; I commanded this canal to be dug from the Nile to the sea that goes from Persia, and ships passed from Egypt by it to Persia. A king in Iran was linking the Mediterranean world to his own coast.

dating_basis: Darius Persepolis d (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13) is in Darius's name and undated; the range is his reign per Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 13-14 (read this session). reliability=medium.
title_en: Darius inscribes the terrace wall at Persepolis
summary_en: On the retaining wall of the new palace terrace Darius wrote that Ahura Mazda made him king, that Persia was a land of good horses and good men that feared no enemy, and asked the god to protect it from three things: a hostile army, famine, and the Lie.

dating_basis: Darius Naqsh-i Rustam a (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13) is in Darius's first person and undated; the range is his reign per Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 13-14 (read this session). Its province list includes India, so it is later than the Behistun list (see W_DNA); that is not narrowed into the range. reliability=medium.
title_en: Darius's tomb façade is inscribed at Naqsh-i Rustam
summary_en: Above the rock-cut tomb Darius set out who he was — a Persian, son of a Persian, an Aryan — the peoples who bore his throne, and a last instruction to whoever reads it: what is the command of Ahura Mazda, let it not seem repugnant to you; do not leave the right path; do not sin.

dating_basis: Herodotus 6.43-45 (read 2026-09-13): 'at the beginning of spring' after the suppression of the Ionian revolt, Mardonius came down to the coast, sailed round Athos and lost about three hundred ships and twenty thousand men. No year is given. The range sits after the fall of Miletus (merged E_GR_015, 494) and before the expedition that ended at Marathon (merged E_GR_017, 490). reliability=medium.
title_en: Mardonius's fleet is wrecked off Mount Athos
summary_en: On his way to punish Eretria and Athens, Mardonius deposed the tyrants of the Ionian cities and set up democracies, then lost much of his fleet to a north wind off Athos while Thracians mauled his army in Macedonia. The expedition turned back; the next one went by sea to Marathon.

dating_basis: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 14 (read 2026-09-13): the last tablets of Darius's 36th year run to September-November 486 and Xerxes is king by 1 December 486. Herodotus 7.4 (read this session): Darius died in the year after the Egyptian revolt, 'after a reign of six and thirty years in all'. The Perseus English at 7.4.1 prints an inline '521-485' that is an editorial note, not Herodotus, and is not used.
title_en: Darius I dies and Xerxes becomes king
summary_en: Darius died while preparing to punish both Egypt and Athens, after thirty-six years on the throne. He had already named Xerxes, his son by Cyrus's daughter Atossa, as heir over an elder son born before he was king.

dating_basis: Herodotus 7.7 (read 2026-09-13): 'Xerxes first marched against the rebels in the year after Darius' death'. Darius's death is November 486 (E_PE_021), so the following year is 485, and the range allows the Persian regnal year to run into 484.
title_en: Xerxes reconquers Egypt
summary_en: The new king's first campaign was not against Greece but against Egypt, which had revolted in Darius's last years. Herodotus says Xerxes laid it under a harsher slavery than before and made his brother Achaemenes its governor.
note: The quotation of Herodotus 7.7.1 in dating_basis supplies an apostrophe: the PerseusDL perseus-eng2 file reads 'in the year after Darius death' (re-read 2026-10-13).

dating_basis: Herodotus 7.22 (read 2026-09-13): 'for about three years' preparations had been under way at Athos, the digging done by men under the lash; 7.37.1 (read this session): the canal was reported finished before the army wintered and set out from Sardis in spring. That spring is the 480 campaign (8.51.1, Calliades archon, as on the merged E_GR_019/020). The range counts back about three years from 480.
title_en: Xerxes has a canal dug through the isthmus of Athos
summary_en: Remembering the fleet lost off Athos, Xerxes had a ship canal cut across the neck of the peninsula, wide enough for two triremes rowed abreast. Herodotus thought it pride: the ships could have been dragged across.

dating_basis: Herodotus 7.33-37 (read 2026-09-13): the bridges were built from Abydos, broken by a storm, rebuilt, and reported finished before the army wintered at Sardis and marched to Abydos 'at the beginning of spring'; 8.51.1 (read this session) dates the arrival in Attica to the archonship of Calliades, 480/479 by CAL_ARCHON as on the merged E_GR_020. The range covers building in 481 and crossing in 480.
title_en: Xerxes bridges the Hellespont, and has the sea whipped
summary_en: Two bridges of boats were laid from Abydos across to Europe. When a storm broke them, Xerxes ordered the strait given three hundred lashes and addressed as 'bitter water', and had the overseers beheaded. New bridges held, and the army crossed into Europe.

dating_basis: Herodotus 8.113-117 (read 2026-09-13): a few days after Salamis Xerxes marched away, left Mardonius in Thessaly, reached the crossing in forty-five days, found the bridges broken and crossed to Abydos by ship, and came to Sardis. Salamis is 480 on the merged E_GR_021 (archon Calliades, CAL_ARCHON).
title_en: Xerxes retreats from Greece to Sardis
summary_en: After the defeat at Salamis the king left Mardonius with an army in Greece and went home by land. Herodotus says he reached the Hellespont with almost nothing of his host, found the bridges gone, crossed by ship, and lost more men to overeating and bad water before reaching Sardis.

dating_basis: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 15 (read 2026-09-13): a Persepolis text shows Xerxes alive in his year 20, months X-XII (which end 24 March 465), and an Elephantine papyrus of 3 January 464 is dated 'year 21, the accession year of Artaxerxes', so he was dead and succeeded before the end of 465. Diodorus 11.69 (Loeb vol. IV via LacusCurtius, read this session) puts the murder in the archonship of Lysitheus; 11.70.1 puts the 79th Olympiad in the following archonship, and Ol. 79.1 = 464/463 by CAL_OLYMPIAD, so Lysitheus is 465/464 — consistent. The narrative of the murder is Diodorus's, four centuries later, hence reliability=medium.
title_en: Xerxes is murdered and Artaxerxes I takes the throne
summary_en: Diodorus tells it as a palace plot: the captain of the guard, Artabanus, killed Xerxes at night, persuaded the young Artaxerxes that his brother Darius was the murderer, and had him kill his brother — then turned on Artaxerxes himself and was killed by him. The dated documents show only that Xerxes died in 465 and Artaxerxes succeeded.

dating_basis: Thucydides 1.137-138 (Crawley, read 2026-09-13): Themistocles wrote to 'King Artaxerxes, Xerxes's son, who had just come to the throne', asked a year's grace to learn Persian, came to court at the end of the year, was given Magnesia, Lampsacus and Myus, and died there; 'there is a monument to him in the marketplace of Asiatic Magnesia'. The lower bound is the accession (E_PE_026). Thucydides gives no year for his death; the upper bound is only the year's grace plus a few years, and reliability is medium accordingly.
title_en: Themistocles enters the Persian king's service and governs Magnesia
summary_en: The Athenian who won Salamis, exiled and hunted by the Greeks, wrote to the son of the king he had defeated offering his services. Artaxerxes gave him a year to learn Persian, then made him governor of Magnesia on the Maeander, where he died and where his monument stood in Thucydides's day.

dating_basis: Diodorus 11.71.3-6 (Loeb via LacusCurtius, read 2026-09-13) puts the Egyptian revolt under Inaros in the archonship of Tlepolemus, the second after Lysitheus (465/464; see E_PE_026), hence 463/462. Thucydides 1.104 (Crawley, read this session) narrates the revolt and the Athenian expedition but gives no year, placing it in his sequence after the surrender of Ithome and Megara's alliance with Athens. The range holds Diodorus's year open to the later placement Thucydides's order allows; reliability=medium.
title_en: Egypt revolts from Artaxerxes under Inaros, with an Athenian fleet
summary_en: Inaros, a Libyan king, raised almost all of Egypt against the Persian king and invited Athens in. An Athenian fleet of two hundred ships sailed up the Nile and took two-thirds of Memphis, besieging the Persians in the citadel called the White Castle.

dating_basis: Thucydides 1.109-110 (Crawley, read 2026-09-13): Megabyzus son of Zopyrus besieged the Greeks on the island of Prosopitis for a year and six months, drained the channel and took it, and 'the enterprise of the Hellenes came to ruin after six years of war'. Diodorus 11.77 (read this session) puts the end in the archonship of Phrasicleides, when the 80th Olympiad was celebrated (Ol. 80.1 = 460/459 by CAL_OLYMPIAD). Thucydides gives no starting year. The start is E_PE_028's range, -463/-459 (Diodorus 11.71's archonship of Tlepolemus, held open to Thucydides's order), and six years counted from it end in -457/-453; counted inclusively they end in -458/-454, which the same range holds. The range holds both sources: its lower bound is Diodorus's end-year, -460, and its upper bound is the later end of Thucydides's count, -453. The two disagree by several years, and reliability is low. (Until 2026-10-13 the upper bound was -454, counted from a start in 460, which is Diodorus's end-year and not E_PE_028's start. Thucydides 1.104 and 1.109-110 in the Crawley translation and Diodorus 11.71 and 11.77 re-read 2026-10-13.)
title_en: Megabyzus retakes Egypt and destroys the Athenian force at Prosopitis
summary_en: A Persian army under Megabyzus drove the Greeks out of Memphis, besieged them on an island in the Nile for eighteen months, and then diverted the river so their ships sat on dry land. Egypt returned to the king; Inaros was betrayed and crucified, and a relief squadron from Athens sailed into a trap.

dating_basis: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 15-16 (read 2026-09-13): Artaxerxes I was recognised in Babylonia until the end of December 424 and possibly February 423; Darius II was king by 13 February 423. Thucydides 4.50.3 (Crawley, read this session in both the MIT and the Perseus files): Athenian envoys at Ephesus heard of the death of King Artaxerxes son of Xerxes 'which took place about that time', in the winter that ended the war's seventh year.
title_en: Artaxerxes I dies
summary_en: The king who had received Themistocles and ended the Egyptian revolt died after some forty years on the throne. Athenian envoys on their way to his court heard the news at Ephesus and went home.

dating_basis: Thucydides 8.17.4-18 (Crawley 1874 in the PerseusDL file tlg0003.tlg001.perseus-eng6.xml, read 2026-09-13; the MIT file on SRC_CRAWLEY_THUC stops at 8.7): 'the first alliance between the king and the Lacedaemonians was now concluded immediately upon the revolt of the Milesians, by Tissaphernes and Chalcideus'. The chapter falls in the summer that opens the war's twentieth year (the MIT text's last lines, 8.7, read this session), 412 on Thucydides's count from spring 431 (merged E_GR_029).
title_en: Tissaphernes and Sparta make their first alliance against Athens
summary_en: Just after Miletus revolted from Athens, the Persian governor and the Spartan commander agreed that whatever land the king and his ancestors had held should be the king's, that they would fight Athens jointly and make no separate peace. Thucydides quotes the text in full; its first clause reaches back to whatever the king's ancestors had held.

dating_basis: Thucydides 8.58.1 (Crawley in PerseusDL eng6, read 2026-09-13) dates the convention 'in the thirteenth year of the reign of Darius, while Alexippidas was Ephor at Lacedaemon', in the plain of the Maeander; the chapter falls in the winter that 8.60.3 (read this session) says ended the war's twentieth year, i.e. winter 412/411. Parker & Dubberstein 1942 pp. 15-16 (read this session) give Darius II's accession year as 424/423 (king by February 423), which makes his year 13 run from spring 411 to spring 410 on the Babylonian reckoning. The two readings differ by a few months; the range holds both rather than choosing. This is the one direct synchronism between a Greek war-year and an Achaemenid regnal year read this session.
title_en: A third treaty between Sparta and Persia, dated by the Persian king's reign
summary_en: A convention concluded in the plain of the Maeander between the Spartans and their allies and Tissaphernes, Hieramenes and the sons of Pharnaces, opening with the clause that the king's country in Asia shall be the king's, to treat as he pleases. It is dated first by the thirteenth year of Darius and only second by the Spartan magistrate.

dating_basis: Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 16 (read 2026-09-13): no dated business documents for Darius II's years 14-19; Artaxerxes II recognised before April 404. The same work's conversion tables (pp. 31-32, read 2026-10-13) run Darius II's years 1 to 19 from spring 423 to spring 404 and begin Artaxerxes II's year 1 in April 404; p. 16, directly after the evidence for Darius II, says that from there on the lengths of reigns are established chiefly by the Ptolemaic Canon, and p. 8 that the Canon furnishes the general basis of the whole chronology. (The nineteen years, 423-405, were first read on 2026-09-13 in Ptolemy's Canon as tabulated at livius.org, which has no sources row; that page is named here only as the provenance of that reading.) Xenophon, Anabasis 1.1.1-3 (Brownson, read this session) narrates the deathbed and succession and gives no year.
title_en: Darius II dies; Artaxerxes II succeeds and arrests his brother Cyrus
summary_en: When Darius lay sick and expected to die, he wished to have both his sons with him: the elder, Artaxerxes, was already there, and he summoned the younger, Cyrus, from his province. After Darius's death Tissaphernes accused Cyrus of plotting against the new king; Artaxerxes arrested him, and only their mother's plea sent Cyrus back to his province — where, Xenophon says, he began planning to take the throne.

dating_basis: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.8.26-27 and 1.9.1 (Brownson, read 2026-09-13) narrate the battle and Cyrus's death without a year. The year range is the one the merged E_GR_040 gives the whole march from Hellenica 3.1.2. The place is left blank: the battlefield is not located by anything read this session, and no Pleiades record was found for Cunaxa.
title_en: Cyrus the Younger is killed fighting his brother's army
summary_en: In the battle against his brother's army, Cyrus caught sight of the king, charged with a handful of attendants, and, as Xenophon reports from Ctesias the physician, wounded him through his breastplate; then a javelin struck him below the eye and he was killed, with eight of his noblest companions dead around him. Xenophon calls him the most kingly Persian since Cyrus the Great.

dating_basis: The Cyrus Cylinder (Rogers 1912, pp. 380-384, read 2026-09-13) narrates Cyrus's peaceful entry into Babylon (lines 17-23) — October 539 on the Nabonidus Chronicle and Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) p. 11 (read this session) — and names his son Cambyses as living (lines 27, 35), so it was written before Cyrus's death, reported in Babylon in August 530 (same, p. 12). The text is contemporary; its date is only that window.
title_en: Cyrus proclaims that he has returned gods and peoples to their homes
summary_en: In a clay cylinder written in Babylonian for Babylon, Cyrus presents himself as the king Marduk chose to end Nabonidus's misrule, who entered the city without a battle, and who sent the gods of many cities back to their sanctuaries and gathered their deported people and returned them to their homes.

dating_basis: Xerxes Persepolis a (Tolman 1908, read 2026-09-13) is in Xerxes's name and undated; the range is his reign per Parker & Dubberstein 1942 (SRC_PD1942) pp. 14-15 (read this session).
title_en: Xerxes builds and inscribes the Gate of All Lands at Persepolis
summary_en: Over the winged bulls of the new gateway Xerxes repeated his father's creed — a great god, Ahura Mazda, made earth and heaven and humankind and happiness for humankind — and called the building a colonnade for the representatives of all countries.

dating_basis: Hypothesis V to the Clouds (Codex Venetus), read this session (2026-09-13) in Starkie's edition (SRC_STARKIE1911), both in the Greek he prints and in his translation in Introduction VII: the first Clouds was produced at the Great Dionysia in the archonship of Isarchus, when Cratinus won with the Pytine and Ameipsias came second with the Connus (paraphrased: the OCR of Starkie's English garbles the name of Cratinus's play, and the Greek OCR has two misread words, so neither is quoted). The archon year is converted through Diodorus, not taken from the editor: Diodorus 12.65.1 (Loeb vol. V via LacusCurtius, read this session) makes Isarchus archon in the year 'among the Eleians the Eighty-ninth Olympiad was celebrated', and Ol. 89.1 = 424/423 by CAL_OLYMPIAD. The City Dionysia fall in spring, inside that archon year, hence 423. Starkie's note ('March, 423 B.C.') and Merry 1879 ('423 B.C.') agree but are editors' dates and are not used. The same Hypothesis puts the revised Clouds in the archonship of Aminias and says it was not produced; that is not dated here. reliability=medium: the Hypothesis is a late note, though Starkie judges its first two lines a quotation from Aristotle's Didaskaliai.
title_en: Aristophanes' Clouds, with Socrates on stage, is beaten at the City Dionysia
summary_en: The comedy that put Socrates on stage, carried about and claiming to tread on air, was produced at Athens' great spring festival and lost: Cratinus won, Ameipsias came second. Aristophanes revised the play but it was never staged again. Twenty-four years later, at his trial, Socrates told the jurors that they had seen that Socrates for themselves.

title_en: Zhi Bo is defeated at Jinyang
summary_en: Three of the great ministerial houses of Jin — Wei, Han and Zhao — beat Zhi Bo, the strongest of them, at Jinyang. Sima Qian's table records the defeat three times over, once in each victor's column, and tells none of the story: not the siege, not how Wei and Han came to be on the other side from the ally they had marched with the year before. What it does give is the year, and the year is the point — this is where the northern hegemon of the Spring and Autumn annals stops being a state with one master.

title_en: Wei, Han and Zhao divide the lands of Zhi Bo
summary_en: With Zhi Bo beaten, the three surviving houses split his territory between them — 與魏、韓三分其地, 'with Wei and Han divided his lands in three', which is the whole of what the table says. It is the estate of the loser that is divided here, not yet the state of Jin: that comes half a century later, in the same table, when the three are first ranked as feudal lords. Later historians open the Warring States either at this year or at that one; this atlas asserts neither and records the two lines.

title_en: The nine cauldrons shake
summary_en: The nine cauldrons were the regalia of the Zhou house, the vessels in which the mandate to rule was supposed to sit. In the twenty-third year of King Weilie the table records, in four characters, that they shook. It is the only thing the Zhou column has to say about the year in which three of the king's ministers' ministers became lords in their own right, two columns to the right on the same line.

summary_en: Three columns of one line each read 初為侯 — 'first made a marquis' — and the Chu column glosses the year for all three: 魏、韓、趙始列為諸侯. The houses that had divided Zhi Bo's lands fifty years earlier are now states with a rank in the Zhou order, and Jin is no longer one of the states this table follows. The cells record the new standing and name nobody who granted it.

title_en: Marquis Wen of Wei receives the classics from Zixia
summary_en: The line that carries the Wei court's reputation: the new marquis takes instruction in the classics from Zixia, one of Confucius's own disciples, and bows from his carriage every time he passes the street where the recluse Duangan Mu lives. It is the earliest picture in this table of a Warring States ruler courting the scholars rather than commanding them — and it is chronologically very hard, because the Shiji elsewhere makes Zixia about a hundred years old by this date.

title_en: Lu taxes the fields by the mu for the first time
summary_en: Three characters in the Lu annal mark the first known land tax: instead of taking the produce of a lord's field worked in common, the state of Lu began to tax cultivated land by its area. The commentary calls it a breach of ritual. It is the first step in the series by which Lu moved from lineage dues to state extraction. Placed on the map at Qufu, the capital, as the seat of the court that decided it; the source names no place.
note: THIN ON INTERPRETATION (flag carried from r8-3, as ruled): the event is certain (a one-line entry in the Lu court annal) but what 稅畝 actually changed is not described in any source read. The classic gives three characters; the Zuo commentary gives one sentence of judgement and the principle it breaks (穀出不過藉); the Hanshu gloss is Han-era. The summary's 'tax by area' is the plain sense of 稅畝 and goes no further. title_en: Lu levies armour by the qiu
summary_en: Four years after the land tax, Lu began to levy armour and military equipment by the qiu, a rural unit of several villages, in response to the threat from Qi. Military obligation was being reassessed on the land itself rather than on the noble houses. Placed on the map at Qufu, the capital, as the seat of the court that decided it; the source names no place.

title_en: Lu forms three armies and the three great houses divide the ducal levy
summary_en: Ji Wuzi proposed three armies, one for each of the three great ministerial houses, each to tax its own; the houses swore to it, divided the duke's forces into three and took one each. Each then reorganised the levy of its share differently, and the Ji house exempted those who entered its service. Military power in Lu passed from the duke to the houses. Placed on the map at Qufu, the capital, as the seat of the court that decided it; the source names no place.

title_en: Lu levies the military tax by the field, over Confucius's objection
summary_en: The head of the Ji house wanted to levy the military tax on every field, and sent Confucius's disciple Ran Qiu to sound him out. Confucius refused to answer in public, then told Ran Qiu privately that a gentleman takes the lightest levy and that even this one would not satisfy greed; if the Ji wanted precedent, the statutes of the Duke of Zhou existed. title_en: Zheng kills Deng Xi and adopts his bamboo law code
summary_en: Deng Xi had written a penal code of his own on bamboo strips. Si Chuan, who governed Zheng, had him killed and then put his code into use. title_en: Jin and Chu swear the first truce outside the west gate of Song
summary_en: Brokered by Hua Yuan of Song, who was on good terms with leaders on both sides, envoys of the two great powers swore a written covenant at Song: neither would make war on the other, each would come to the other's help, the roads would stay open, and the spirits would destroy whoever broke it. It is the first text of an interstate non-aggression covenant in the record. Within a few years the two powers were at war again.

title_en: Xiang Xu's conference at Song: the states swear to stop the wars
summary_en: Thirty-three years after the first truce, Xiang Xu of Song persuaded Jin, Chu, Qi, Qin and the smaller states to send delegates to Song and swear to end the wars among them. Jin's minister gave the reason: war ruins the people, eats the state's wealth and is the great calamity of small states. The chronicle does not polish it: Xiang Xu wanted the credit, the Chu delegation came armed under their robes, Jin and Chu disputed who would swear first, and afterwards a Song colleague said that no one can abolish arms.
note: The Zuo's own irony is kept, not smoothed (r8-3 §2): 以為名, 'to make a name', is the motive the chronicle assigns, and 子罕's rebuke (誰能去兵) closes the same year's entry. polity_id blank for the same reason as E_CN_043. Place: the oaths are sworn 於宋西門之外 and 于蒙門之外, both at the Song capital; PL_SHANGQIU is the place the source names.

title_en: Li Kui's policy of making full use of the land, for Marquis Wen of Wei
summary_en: Han historians credit Li Kui with the first worked-out agrarian policy of a Chinese state: a calculation of how much more grain a territory yields when farmed diligently, and a state granary that bought grain in good years and sold it in bad ones so that prices hurt neither townsmen nor farmers. 'It was put into practice in Wei,' the Hanshu says, 'and the state became rich and strong.'

No place: the Wei court's seat in this reign is not established from a source read (POL_WEI's capital_place_id is blank for the same reason).

title_en: Li Kui compiles the Canon of Laws (late tradition)
summary_en: A history compiled under the Tang dynasty, more than a thousand years later, says that Li Kui, teacher of Marquis Wen, collected the laws of the various states into a Canon of Laws in six sections, beginning with theft and violence, and that Shang Yang took it with him when he went to govern Qin. If true, it is the beginning of the code line that runs through Qin into Han law. Nothing earlier names the book.
note: RELIABILITY LOW, AND ITS OWN DATED RELIABILITY (r9-0 task book): the title 法經 and its six sections are attested only in the 晉書 刑法志, a Tang-dynasty compilation; the page is marked Textquality 50% by the wiki. The Han catalogue's 李子三十二篇 shows that a Li-zi book in the legalist class existed in the Han library; it does not name it 法經 or describe it. The Jinshu's chain (Li Kui to Shang Yang to Qin to Han) is the Tang historians' account and is reported as theirs.

title_en: Wu Qi reforms the state of Chu
summary_en: As chief minister of King Dao of Chu, Wu Qi 'made the laws clear and the orders exact': he abolished offices the state did not need, cut off the privileges of royal kinsmen of distant descent, and spent what was saved on soldiers. Han Fei's version of his advice is blunter: the great ministers were too powerful and the enfeoffed lords too many, so fiefs should be taken back after three generations. The program lasted only as long as the king who backed it.

title_en: Wu Qi is killed at the funeral of King Dao of Chu
summary_en: When King Dao died, the nobles whose privileges Wu Qi had cut rose against him. He ran to the king's body and lay on it; the arrows that killed him struck the corpse as well. After the burial the new king had everyone who had shot at the royal body executed, and more than seventy families were wiped out.

title_en: Shang Yang persuades Duke Xiao of Qin to change the laws
summary_en: Over the objections of two senior ministers, who held that the laws of the ancestors should not be changed, Shang Yang told Duke Xiao that 'there is more than one way to govern an age, and serving the state does not require copying antiquity.' The duke gave him office and issued the new laws: households grouped in fives and tens and made liable for one another's crimes, informers rewarded like soldiers who take an enemy head, rank given for military merit and withheld even from members of the ruling house without it, and those who produced the most grain and cloth exempted from labour service. The people, the Shiji says, suffered under the laws at first and after three years found them convenient.

title_en: Qin moves its capital to Xianyang and merges its villages into counties
summary_en: Qin built gate towers and a palace at Xianyang and moved its capital there; it merged its small villages and settlements into counties, each run by an appointed magistrate, reorganised the boundaries of the fields and, in the biography's account, made the measures of grain, weight and length uniform. The county, governed by a salaried appointee instead of a hereditary lord, became the basic unit of the later empire. The Shiji gives two counts of the new counties: thirty-one in two chapters and forty-one in a third.
note: PLACE: Shiji 5 and Shiji 68 name Xianyang for the new capital, so PL_XIANYANG is the source's place for the move; the county reform is the same year's entry and is not separately placed. title_en: Shen Buhai governs Han as chancellor
summary_en: Shen Buhai, a former minor official of Zheng, won over Marquis Zhao of Han with his 'technique' and governed as chancellor until his death: at home he reformed the administration, abroad he managed the other lords, and 'as long as Master Shen lived the state was well governed, its army strong, and no one invaded Han.' Han Fei later judged that he had mastered the ruler's control of officials but never unified Han's laws.

title_en: Shang Yang is killed after Duke Xiao's death
summary_en: When Duke Xiao died, members of the ruling house who hated Shang Yang (he had once had the crown prince's tutor branded for the prince's offence) accused him of plotting rebellion. title_en: Mencius comes to King Hui of Liang
summary_en: Mencius came to the court of King Hui of Wei, known by the name of his capital as the king of Liang. The king, who had lost battles to Qi and Qin, asked what profit his visitor would bring the state. Mencius answered that a ruler who talks of profit teaches his ministers and his people to talk of profit too, until high and low are fighting each other for it: 'Why must Your Majesty speak of profit? There is humaneness and rightness, and that is all.'
note: PLACE, A STATED READING (the task book asks for the Wei capital's own place reading): in Shiji 44 the king says Mencius has come 'to the court of my humble city' (辱幸至獘邑之廷), and the same chapter records in Hui's 31st year, four years before this visit by its own count, that the seat moved to Daliang (安邑近秦，於是徙治大梁); Shiji 68 records the same move (而魏遂去安邑，徙都大梁). title_en: Su Qin persuades Yan to join an alliance against Qin (traditional)
summary_en: According to the Shiji, Su Qin, after years of failure, gained an audience with Marquis Wen of Yan and argued that Yan's safety lay in alliance with its neighbour Zhao. The marquis agreed, and Su Qin went on to persuade Zhao, Han, Wei, Qi and Chu in turn, until he held the chancellor's seals of all six states. How much of this story belongs to Su Qin himself is disputed, by Sima Qian among others.

title_en: Zhang Yi serves as chancellor of Qin

title_en: Han Fei dies in a Qin prison

title_en: Qin unifies the states and divides the realm into thirty-six commanderies
summary_en: With the capture of the king of Qi, Qin had conquered all six of its rivals, and its king took the new title of emperor. His ministers proposed making the emperor's sons kings of the distant conquests; Li Si answered that the Zhou had done exactly that and its kinsmen had ended by fighting each other, and the emperor agreed with him. The realm was divided instead into thirty-six commanderies, each under an appointed governor, commandant and inspector; the weapons of the conquered were melted down at Xianyang, measures, weights and axle widths made uniform, the script standardised, and 120,000 rich households moved to the capital.
note: CATEGORY: reform, for the settlement; the conquest that made it possible (得齊王建) is recorded in the same entry and not split into a second row. title_en: Bimbisara asks the order not to ordain the king's soldiers
summary_en: Unrest breaks out on Magadha's frontier, and soldiers ordered there go forth as monks instead, so as not to do evil in battle. The king's judges name the penalty for ordaining a royal servant: the preceptor's head, the proclaimer's tongue, and half the ribs of the group. Bimbisara takes the matter to the Buddha, and a rule follows: no one employed by a king is to be given the going forth.
note: place_id blank: pli-tv-kd1:40 names no place for the scene. The decree is the order's own rule, made at a king's request; category decree is used for the rule, not for a royal edict.

title_en: Bimbisara proposes the fortnightly assembly, on the rival sects' model
summary_en: Wanderers of other religions meet on the eighth, fourteenth and fifteenth days of the half-month to teach, and win supporters by it. King Bimbisara suggests that the Buddha's monks gather on the same days, and the Buddha allows it. One of the order's lasting institutions, the observance day, begins as a king's idea copied from the competition.

title_en: Mahapajapati Gotami is ordained: the order of nuns begins
summary_en: The Buddha's aunt asks three times at Kapilavatthu for women to be allowed to go forth and is refused. She cuts her hair, puts on ochre robes and walks to Vesali with a group of Sakyan women. Ananda pleads for them, and the Buddha agrees on condition that she accept eight important principles that subordinate nuns to monks. He then says that because women have gone forth the true teaching will last five hundred years instead of a thousand.

title_en: Ajatasattu defeats Pasenadi in Kasi
summary_en: King Ajatasattu of Magadha marches on Kasi with an army of four divisions; King Pasenadi of Kosala marches out to defend it, is defeated, and withdraws to his capital Savatthi. Hearing of it, the Buddha says: Victory breeds enmity; the defeated sleep badly.
note: polity_id blank: an interstate war has two sides, and the row does not choose one. place_id is Kasi, the contested country, which is unlocated in this dataset.

title_en: Pasenadi defeats and captures Ajatasattu, then lets him go
summary_en: In a second battle over Kasi, Pasenadi defeats Ajatasattu and takes him alive. Because Ajatasattu is his nephew, he confiscates his elephants, cavalry, chariots and infantry and lets him go with his life. The Buddha's verse: the plunderer is plundered.

title_en: Ajatasattu fortifies Rajagaha against King Pajjota
summary_en: Not long after the Buddha's death, King Ajatasattu of Magadha, suspicious of King Pajjota, has his capital Rajagaha fortified, and his chief minister Vassakara is out supervising the work when he stops to question Ananda about who leads the order now.

title_en: The first communal recitation at Rajagaha
summary_en: Five hundred senior monks spend the rains at Rajagaha to fix the teaching together. Mahakassapa questions Upali on the monastic law and Ananda on the discourses, and the monastic law's account says the five collections were recited. When the monk Purana arrives afterwards from the Southern Hills, he calls it well recited, and says he will nevertheless remember what he himself heard from the Buddha.

title_en: Sariputta's recitation at Pava, after the Jain split
summary_en: In the Mallas' new town hall at Pava, the Buddha's back is sore and he asks Sariputta to speak. The Jain teacher has just died at Pava and his followers have split into quarrelling factions. Sariputta draws the lesson: the monks should all recite the teaching in concert, without disputing, so that the path lasts, and he sets it out in numbered lists. The Buddha approves.
